The precision of B^0_s lifetime assessments will significantly improve with the anticipated LHC Run 2 dataset, which will gather a 250 $b\bar b$ events per picosecond at the $b\bar b$ threshold. To make full use of this data set, the LHCb upgrade is necessary, which will enhance the LHCb detector's capabilities. The proposed upgrade will enable the collection of the entire Run 2 dataset and surpass the capabilities present at mid-run, particularly the production rate and data acquisition system. The upgraded detector will also be capable of studying rare hadron flavor processes involving $B^0_s$ mesons and charmed particles. The new features of the upgraded detector will be presented, with the parameters for muon triggers and vertex detector modifications being discussed in detail. The upgrade's impact on the measurement of the $B^0_s$ lifetime and the reasons behind the design of the hadron calorimeter will also be presented. The design of the upgrade will be shown, with the hadron calorimeter being a key addition. The impact of the upgrade on $B^0_s$ lifetime measurements and rare decay modes will be presented, with predictions for commissioning data at 11.5 TeV and datasets of 50 fb$^{-1}$ and 300 fb$^{-1}$ being discussed.

This research focuses on formulating and resolving a stochastic control problem within the framework of Itô diffusion, subject to partial observation.  To address this issue, a discrete version of the control problem is created and its convergence is analyzed.  Furthermore, we establish that, under specific conditions, the solution to the discrete problem converges to the solution of the original problem as the discretization approaches continuity.  Our approach involves creating a probabilistic representation for the controlled cost and demonstrating that the cost can be represented in terms of the state's behavior under the probability measure, which allows for the use of convergence theorems based on the representation.  Our results provide an alternative method of proving convergence based on the problem's setting, in this case, by using the convergence of probability measures in the Wasserstein distance.  Our research also has an applied component, in that we examine the convergence of the problem when friction between tires and roads is present in the singular stochastic control problem presented in Carmona and Delarue's 2018 book.  Our analysis provides a demonstration of how to use results from the paper by Daneri and Sosa Wagner 2021 concerning the convergence of solutions to stochastic differential equations with less regular data.

The search for anisotropy in the high-energy cosmic ray sky is being intensified, with the anisotropic pattern expected to offer clues about the origin of diffuse extragalactic background radiation. Theoretical models predict that the anisotropy structure changes from dipolar to clumped patterns as energy rises above 4 EeV due to the limited access to observations of the dipole beyond 10 EeV. The authors of this study utilized data from the Telescope Array, covering 44 TeVnr of exposure, and have used a statistical method that accounts for both experimental and intrinsic random variations in the cosmic ray distribution. The observed anisotropy is energy-dependent and may be associated with the origin of the diffuse background radiation. This research shows that certain key properties associated with infinite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, specifically nilpotency and solvability, also apply to their finite-dimensional counterparts. Furthermore, it establishes a direct correlation between the Zinbiel upper and lower series and a solvability series of finite-dimensional algebras.

The connection between flow fluctuations and the collective behavior observed in heavy-ion collisions is explored. Specifically, the relationships between higher-order flow coefficients and particle number in collisions are examined to infer the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. A simple model is utilized to investigate how the relation between flow coefficients and transverse momentum can reveal information about the quantum state of matter. Furthermore, a framework is proposed to analyze non-Gaussian distributions of transverse momentum by considering the interplay between heavy-ion collisions and quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the potential for extracting physical parameters from non-Gaussian measurements is discussed, particularly through the use of cumulative distributions and their relation to hadron yield fluctuations.

Our research focuses on consistent answer estimation for acyclic CQs under the closed world assumption for intact facts within incomplete databases defined by repairs. We aim to determine the smallest probability assignment that would make a certain answer valid. For a specific subset of first-order formulas, under the CWA, we establish consistent answers in a four-valued logic framework. We prove that determining appropriate probability assignments for FOMs within this subset is doable in PTIME, while other cases involve higher computational complexities: NP^NP and PNP^cP for dpt. Furthermore, we establish that for first-order logic, determining consistent answers for databases with incomplete relations is undecidable, but for relational databases, it is undecidable under certain conditions.

This research focuses on nonlinear modeling using a Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive model with external variables (TV-PARX). We develop and analyze a new time series model that can adapt to changes in underlying structure by incorporating external variables, allowing for flexible coefficients in certain variables to capture structural breaks. Gaps in the data are handled through an innovative missing data algorithm. The new TV-PARX model is extensively evaluated through numerical experiments and compared to existing nonlinear models in a detailed study.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) as a possible approach to task representation, enabling robust space and action state generalization for task execution. Our primary goal is to enable robots with limited space and action state generalization capabilities to execute new tasks by inputting demonstration data. To achieve this, we develop a neural field that maps object configurations to outputs suitable for neural networks, allowing multiple instances of objects to be handled efficiently. Our method also allows input sensory data, enabling networks to handle tasks without sensory inputs as well as with them. We objectify our approach to task representation and demonstrate a manipulation learning framework in simulation and on a real robot. Our framework enables learning tasks from single-instance demonstrations and generalizes to instance- and state-space variations, and in a real-world setting, learns tasks from first-person visual input in the form of object trajectories, and generalizes to instances without prior exposure, even in the absence of visual input.

Researchers exploring the large N limit of three-dimensional QCD using the Laplace expansion have discovered a critical point at $z_c$ with its value depending on the number of dimensions $N$. Specifically, they found that for a two-glu理论 model, $|z_c|$ increases as it approaches three-dimensional space, where $|z_c|=1$ and $|z_c|<1$ for one- and four-dimensional models, respectively. To better understand these findings, a new matrix model was created based on the Laplace transformation and analyzed both numerically and through perturbative methods. By comparing the results, the model's critical point $|z_c|$ matches the expectations set by the one- and two-glu理论 models and is found to move towards one when the number of fermion types is near two, but shifts beyond one when there are four types. Furthermore, a general formula for $|z_c|$ in the fermionic matrix model with $N$ types was derived through perturbation analysis, confirming the model's behavior in the limit of a very large N.

In this paper, we demonstrate that, given a dataset affected by $Z_2$-symmetry and additve noise, the ability of the TAP free energy to accurately reflect data-signalling leads to the convergence of the TAP algorithm's gradient descent. To achieve this, we first show that, at a certain point, the TAP algorithm's iteration matches the optimal solution's accuracy and occurs when the noise level exceeds a specific threshold. Following this, the TAP free energy's dynamics are tracked, either leading to a minimum corresponding to the unique solution or, if noise is too high, failing to reach a minimum that represents a valid solution. Ultimately, our analysis of the TAP free energy's behavior is aligned with the convergence of the approximate message passing algorithm's iteration.

The recent breakthrough in wide-field photography allows for the determination of aerosol optical depth in various directions, dependent on the Earth's atmospheric position relative to the observed object, all without requiring absolute signal normalization. This significant achievement was initially demonstrated using photographs of Venus taken by multiple observatories, yielding a measurement of optical depth relative to the zenith at 0.14±0.02 for 0-degree to 80-degree vertical solar angle observations. To replicate these results, we developed an radiative transfer model that simulates atmospheric reflection and enables the extraction of optical depth values directly from wide-field photography. Estimating the pose of objects without known 3D models by using single images remains a challenging task, particularly when the known objects are part of a larger set defined by their semantic category and object pose parameters are confined within known priors for each individual instance. To address this issue, we propose a novel optimization-based method that groups projected 2D points from the image and estimates the pose of objects known within a scene. Each projected point is semantically anchored and contributes to exactly one projection group, which in turn is also assigned to exactly one world frame-located object. We employ a cost function that considers the number of points, projection groups, and instances, as well as the distances between image points to projection curves, their current groups' centroids, and distinctness among groups and instances. As a result, our method achieves accurate pose estimation of multiple instance objects within a single image scene, as demonstrated in experiments with both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Initially, Graphical Lasso was devised to analyze fully observed Gaussian variables. Later adaptations were made to handle missing data and latent variables. In this study, we extend the basic Graphical Lasso framework to incorporate latent variables. We reformulate this extension by adding auxiliary variables back into the optimization process, which can be seen as a flexible penalty method. We examine this penalty from both its mathematical properties and practical application perspectives. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the capability of our approach to identify valid probability spaces along with corresponding Gaussian graphs that data can exist within.

This research compares three simulation approaches, specifically molecular dynamics simulations using the GROMACS package with three distinct numerical methods. The methods analyzed were velocity Verlet, leapfrog, and the native integrator, each with a focus on accuracy and computational performance. The accuracy of simulations was validated by examining the potential energy landscape of alanine dipeptide in water. Results showed that velocity Verlet and leapfrog integrators maintained the correct potential energy landscape, while the native integrator failed to do so. Furthermore, velocity Verlet and leapfrog integrators exhibited nearly identical potential energy distributions and minimal differences in sampling comparison with production runs. When examining computational efficiency, velocity Verlet outperformed leapfrog and the native integrator in terms of runtime, primarily due to memory access patterns. These findings have significant implications for selecting appropriate numerical methods in large-scale, high-accuracy molecular dynamics simulations.

The concept of node significance in multi-layer networks goes beyond the sum of a node's centrality measures in each individual layer, as it takes into account connections between network layers. The computation of between-layer centrality is supported by the use of between-layer metrics, which can be applied to various network layers. The calculation of these metrics is influenced by the strength of connections between layers and can be derived from the combined adjacency matrices of all layers. The sum of multi-layer networks serves as a framework for the development of centrality metrics that can be applied to network layers with varying levels of connectivity. The relationship between the network layers and their corresponding centrality metrics is examined, and it is shown that increasing connectivity between layers results in heightened note centrality in each layer, which can be noted by the use of lower and upper centrality limits. The network layer connectivity metric serves as a means of assessing network layer centrality and is examined with respect to random network layer models.

We apply a transformation to the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski space,
resulting in a radial equation and analyzing its connection to the Dirac

This study delved into the complexities of surface seal behavior within a cavity at the mouthpiece of a double-reed instrument, taking into account the effect of pressure changes on the instrument's sound and pacing. By modifying an existing one-dimensional model, a two-dimensional model was created to capture the influence of end correction due to varying pressure inside the cavity. The results of nonlinear simulations showed that as the instrument's pacing became more pronounced, the pressure inside the cavity dropped significantly, influencing the pacing speed and depth. To validate the model, nonlinear oscillations were simulated and compared to experimental data, which indicated that the model could reproduce key features of instrument pacing, including a key frequency transition point. The study also proposed a lower threshold pressure that, if exceeded, would prevent pacing and influenced the model's threshold pressure, which was higher than expected. The research highlighted the importance of end correction at the mouthpiece and its role in driving pressure waves, which could help explain the role of air resistance in the frequency transition point. Ultimately, the developed model provided a valuable tool for predicting the pacing behavior of instruments and for exploring new performance techniques, including possible applications in music therapy.

In 1995, Edward Witten proposed a groundbreaking idea in quantum gravity, suggesting that the existence of a minimally charged state dictates the entire spectrum of charged states. This hypothesis relied on the generalized Witten effect, which shows that the number of charged states increases as the external field strength becomes stronger. We verify the validity of the whole predicted spectrum, based on the generalized Witten effect, for N=2 supergravity. Furthermore, we illustrate that the generalized Wu term, which arises from integrating a boundary term in the action, plays a crucial role in determining the characteristics of the states at the higher mass end of the spectrum.

Selenium cubanite, recently observed in the meteorite NWA 7325, exhibits unusual properties including a wide range of electrical charges, mechanical strength, and both paramagnetic and ferromagnetic characteristics. To understand these characteristics on an atomic level, we used state-averaged time-dependent density functional theory to analyze its unique time-reversed configuration, which shows minimal catalytic activity and a substantial charge of three times its atomic mass, according to high-level calculations. This is possible due to the absence of charge exchange between its two key molecular orbitals, which have both paramagnetic and feromagnetic characteristics and are separated by approximately nine electron volts. These features, along with another orbital that is either occupied or empty, form a robust, approximately triangular connection with the surface of the crystal lattice and are responsible for the stability of its configuration, the ease with which it can gain or lose electrons, and its ability to maintain its magnetic characteristics despite being incorporated into the compound.

We investigate the quantum dynamics of a single two-level system interacting with a cavity,
introduced by a material with piezoelectric properties. The interaction between the system and the
cavity is modulated by an external driving force at the Rabi frequency. By analyzing the
Rabi oscillations, the parameters of the cavity can be deduced from the patterns of sidebands
resulting from the oscillations. The amplitude of Rabi oscillations varies significantly with
certain parameters, particularly the driving frequency. We demonstrate that precise control
over a quantum dot can be achieved by fine-tuning the driving frequency. Notably, by
approaching a specific frequency without reaching resonance, the interaction between the
quantum dot and the cavity can be effectively switched on and off. This research provides
robust methods for managing quantum dot-cavity interactions and offers reliable approaches
to manipulating Rabi sideband patterns for accurate determination of Rabi frequencies.

We analyze a Hohenberg-Herbert-Herringbone lattice, modifying the standard HH pattern by introducing a row with horizontal sites in a HH Hamiltonian. By adjusting the energy parameters in this model, we demonstrate that it is possible to control the transmission of light between specific lattice sites. Furthermore, we explore the effects of these interactions on entanglement between photonic qubits within the lattice and show how the transmission of entanglement can be managed through the model's parameters. By applying a specific set of parameters, we induce a transition from an isolated state to a robustly transmitted state when light must traverse the lattice's isolated site. Additionally, we investigate the transmission of a parabolic state within the lattice and find that, unlike other state patterns, it can pass through the isolated site without being affected.

We examine the potential of single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) to investigate the differences in outcome probabilities and the resulting state structures when a single photon acts as a catalyst in various two-port quantum devices, including beam splitters and nonlinear crystals used in spontaneous four-wave mixing (SFWM). 

Our analysis of success probabilities, conditioned on detecting a single photon in specific output modes, reveals distinct outcomes based on the detection setup, the initial coherent state energy, and the loss characteristics of the catalysis device. Notably, we observe that the probability of a particular outcome can surpass that of the corresponding vacuum catalyzed case. 

Furthermore, our study of the resulting state structure reveals that outcomes from SPCCS generated via SFWM share similarities with those from SPCCS generated via beam splitters, including an infinite photon number expansion in contrast to the finite photon number found in the beam splitter scenario. This infinite photon number is gradually suppressed as detection efficiency declines, and we find that the SPCCS resulting from SFWM exhibits an overcompleteness property, enabling any pure state to be represented as an integral of these SPCCSs. 

Overall, our findings provide valuable insights into the unique properties and applications of SPCCSs, and may have implications for the development of efficient quantum technologies.

This paper proposes a novel deep learning framework, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), for image segmentation. The DDAUnet addresses key limitations of existing Unet architectures by incorporating attention mechanisms, dense connections, and dilated convolutions. Attention mechanisms enable the network to focus on relevant features while suppressing irrelevant ones, the dense Unet structure facilitates information exchange between skip links, and dilated convolutions facilitate long-range feature interactions without increasing dimensionality. Experimental results on two public datasets demonstrate the superiority of the DDAUnet over state-of-the-art methods in terms of performance metrics such as Dice Similarity Coefficient, Hausdorff Distance, and 95% HD.

Language translation tools, language models and other components of computational language research help organizations provide better healthcare, legal aid and education services to multilingual communities, among other benefits. Our report outlines real-world advantages of this research for society at large and the potential drawbacks of developing these technologies on public data, including financial, environmental and privacy-related concerns, as well as the significant computational resources required for state-of-the-art models. We explore various approaches to making green, efficient and accessible language technology, and call for industry leaders to set transparency standards for NLP projects, establish industry guidelines, develop NLP systems that prioritize efficiency, make NLP technology more accessible, and create industry-led initiatives to manage NLP research's positive impact on society.

The creation of descriptive text for images has been undertaken for decades, producing vast amounts of data that primarily serves the needs of visually impaired users. Despite this, guidelines for labeling and categorizing images remain largely subjective and unstructured. Due to the exponential growth of image data, there's an pressing requirement for more meaningful and well-defined annotation criteria. We propose the introduction of the Lexically Ordered Sentence Generation task, which entails generating precise, high-quality descriptions that fully capture the visual content of an image. We manually created a comprehensive guide to facilitate image description and presented a baseline model based on convolutional neural networks for LGIT text generation. We conducted multiple evaluation methods, including various text generation metrics, a specialized classification model, and a visually based sample generation model. The results demonstrate that our LGIT task and associated evaluation methods effectively assess the quality of automatic image descriptions and distinguish between visually similar and distinct samples.

A recent investigation into various tantalum oxide phases, including TaO$_2$ and TaO$_3$, has been conducted. By accurately accounting for local field effects, anharmonic vibrations, and spin-electron coupling in a simulated environment, the energy loss properties of electrons were computed using many-body perturbation theory. Comparing the calculated results with experimental optical absorption and infrared absorption data shows that for certain compounds, particularly those with high symmetry and minimal radial electron over-shelling, the harmonic approximation provides a reasonably accurate prediction of optical absorption spectra. However, for other phases, angrite, and ta-oxides, including those with low symmetry and strong electron interaction, we found that the harmonic approximation results significantly differ from actual measurements, and thus, we observed strong agreement with experimental data after incorporating the optical anharmonicity effect.

A recent significant event highlighted how easily misinformation can spread, particularly among users in politically divided regions. This paper outlines an model to simulate the propagation of fake information and presents a way to test this model by using online activity from geographically segregated regions. To study "The Big Sort" effect, which is the tendency for people to fully align themselves with their existing political beliefs, researchers used a Bayesian inference framework and found strong evidence of its existence. This alignment with existing political views accelerates the spread of misinformation but also increases its detection. Consequently, the most suitable indicator for measuring how often users share misinformation is one that considers both propagation and detection rates, rather than just one of those factors in isolation.

We conducted a series of teaching experiments where agents with varying backgrounds instructed humans on navigating a virtual environment for a navigational task. To evaluate how factors such as varying demonstration methods, instructions for using audio cues, different subtasks, and errors influenced the semantic concepts conveyed in speech during teaching, we analyzed the acoustic properties of the language produced by our agents. To systematically assess the impact of these variables on specific acoustic features, we designed a set of machine learning models. The results revealed that both the accuracy of communication and the neural representations of this communication are affected by the errors made, as well as the way in which agents navigate their surrounding environment.

This research paper explores optimal pathing for a non-linear Dirac field when moving between two field configurations, derived from a variational principle based on the bi-Hamiltonian structure of Euler-Poincar\'e2 equations. Calculating this path involves solving a transformed version of the Hamilton-Jacobi variational problem and finding the Euler-Arnold equations for the transformed path. Numerical results for the optimal path of the field are also presented.

While ensuring the reliable operation of sophisticated conversational systems depends heavily on comprehensive and effective testing, developing such testing frameworks is a complicated task. Existing methodologies are prone to instability, with even minor model testing updates often necessitating substantial revisions to testing frameworks. In this study, we propose a straightforward and modular testing framework that automatically generates and manages testing fixtures by leveraging Amazon Web Services, significantly minimizing overhead during model testing. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework enables large-scale testing, with our team successfully conducting over a 100,000 exchanges in a real-world chatbot project. Furthermore, this framework offers added benefits such as enhanced security and speed during tests, as well as the flexibility to create cross-region and model tests.

A critical challenge in recommendation systems is capturing implicit user preferences, which are often complex and diverse. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach called Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE), which captures the interactions between different aspects and learns more comprehensive and representative aspects with lower latency. Specifically, we introduce two aspects preference learning modules: the First, the Side Information Aggregation (SIA) module captures complementary complementary aspects by combining information from multiple sources. Alongside, the GAPE module captures interactive aspects and more latent aspects preference by integrating the interactions among various aspects. To capture the interactions, we employ a Gated Network that regulates the flow of information based on the relationship between different aspects. To validate the effectiveness of GAPE, we design four recommendation tasks and conduct extensive experiments, which show that GAPE achieves superior performance compared to 19 state-of-the-art multi-aspect baseline methods in four aspect generation tasks and 35 recommendation tasks. Furthermore, GAPE exhibits more significant performance improvements in high-latency ratings prediction tasks. Additionally, we further GAPE with five multi-aspect specific modules and achieve even better performance, which enables GAPE to capture more comprehensive aspects' information and outperforms 50 side information-based recommendation models.

This transformation can lead to significant improvements in solution methods, exemplified by the success of the native format for semidefinite programming in achieving low F** barriers*. This study introduces several such natural formulations using the exotic cones derived from the knapsack polytope, balancing their reduced dimensions* with adequate efficiency**, and the combination of these formats can yield favorable results**, bridging the gap between naturally formulated* and highly efficient* approaches*. This strategy can be effectively demonstrated by producing more effective formulations for the single-row integer programming problem and the knapsack polytope cutting plane, exhibiting respectively 15% and 33% reduction in dimensions*, while adhering to acceptable efficiency** criteria,.

The performance of deep neural networks is heavily influenced by the data they are trained on, especially when it comes to medical images, whose variability can be quite substantial. In this study, we investigate the impact of training dataset composition on fully supervised MRI classification tasks, specifically by re-evaluating publicly available datasets with a novel, highly diverse and unseen MRI variability. To this end, we selected three public datasets and conducted multiple evaluations, utilizing three different variations of a U-Net model, trained on combinations of datasets that differed in their variability. Our results show that high diversity in training data, consisting of highly variable and unseen types of variability, leads to superior generalization, even when models are trained on complex data distributions. Furthermore, we discover that including data with broader ranges of variability, such as different resolution sizes, leads to better performance on high-resolution, unseen data. In this context, we also present findings on the critical role of data normalization in training and its varying effects on performance across different models. Ultimately, our study provides valuable insights for selecting training data, particularly when dealing with new, previously unseen data variability.

In recent advancements, network-based optimization techniques have been applied to create networks with desired properties by having agents adjust their positions. These methods generally focus on specific network metrics and offer localized solutions to optimization tasks. We propose a generalized framework of network-based multi-agent optimization problems that encompasses various problems and provide a theoretical framework to analyze them. This framework consists of two parts: a global perspective defining the problem from an overarching viewpoint and a network-based view detailing how a set of agents can collaborate to resolve the problem through position adjustments. We demonstrate the applicability of this framework to multiple problems and examine its benefits, including examining the relationship between the global and network-based views of the objective function, analyzing the convergence of the agent network to the solution, and exploring possible generalizations.

A riis and Chatterjee's (1989) motivation dynamics model explains how agents with varying initial willingness to cooperate can successfully execute a rendezvous strategy. We expanded this model to involve multiple agents, various initial cooperations levels and a more complex environment rendering our approach highly applicable to real-world scenarios. Through a series of experiments with varying agents' cooperation levels and environment complexities, along with a dense grid world for benchmark comparison, our results show that the model can efficiently and robustly execute a rendezvous even when the environment is heavily obscured, at the cost of a moderate time investment. Furthermore, adding or varying initial cooperations among the agents did not considerably impact our method's efficacy or scalability.

We investigated the magnetism in the Gd_x Cm_{1-x}Sn_3 compound series with varying levels of Cm substitution, as the Gd and Cm atoms exhibit very similar magnetic properties. As expected, reducing the content of Cm leads to an increase in the magnetic moment, which is shown by experimental data and supported by a self-atomic-routed approach. As the Cm composition rises, a shift in the magnetism, from being concentrated on the Gd atoms to being focused on the Cm atoms, is observed, and this is also validated by the theoretical findings. The magnetism in these compounds is mainly driven by the interaction between localized electrons on the Gd or Cm atoms, and it can be accurately predicted based on their individual properties. Notably, a significant change in magnetic behavior is not predicted until the Gd content reaches a certain point, where new magnetic states with non-integers per formula unit appear and show a complex interaction between the Gd and Cm atoms.

In 2010, George-Schirer introduced a generalised sign representation for the Coxeter group $W$ with a specific property regarding its descent set. This representation was granted a geometric origin through Brouck's construction in 2014 for the canonical Coxeter system of $W$. This approach established that the generalized standard ordered graphs (OGS) of the Weyl group $B_n$ have fundamental relations that correspond to the Coxeter length within the category of ordered graphs. This Coxeter length was found to satisfy a divisibility condition with $n$ and allows the exchange laws for the generalized sign representation of Weyl group $B_n$ to be expressed in terms of its length and descent set. This analysis is also applicable to crystallographic Coxeter groups that are subgroups of $B_n$ with an adequate set.

The $\cDM$ component in the galactic halo significantly influences the formation, collapse, and the early star formation processes within the galaxy. Theoretical models of the galaxy have the potential to provide critical information about the properties of $\cDM$ dark matter particles. We developed a $\cDM$ simulation based on the $\adobe{N}-body$ method to create an artificial pulsar profile current pulse (APPC) that mirrors real observational data from the pulsar PSR J0952--100. By utilizing the APPC, we performed AP current pulse (APPC) reconstruction and analysis to extract the characteristics of the surrounding halo. We focused on determining the halo's density profile, halo core properties, and the halo sphere properties. These aspects are crucial for comprehending the behavior of $\cDM$ and can guide future research by providing target directions for direct $\cDM$ detection experiments.

The control of quantum computing and sensing systems based on individual Ti-Si colour centres in silicon carbide requires precise understanding of their dynamic behaviour. The spectrum of a single centre can be analysed quickly using fast optical techniques. However, the majority of centres located near the surface show significant speed-dependent frequency changes, which hinders their application in quantum technology. This study investigates optical spectrum evolution over time and speed in a broad range of wavelengths using rapid optical spectroscopy. It reveals that individual centres exhibit speed-dependent frequency shifts that can be matched through models incorporating multiple phonon interactions. Furthermore, groups of centres with varying depths show fast optical spectrum diffusion, which is attributed to photon-induced charge state transitions. These findings provide valuable insights into Ti-Si behaviour and offer new methods for surface defect removal through optical spectrum monitoring and machine learning. However, due to speed-dependent frequency diffusion and speed-induced state transformations, solid-state quantum technology based on Ti-Si colour centres will need defect-free sites through novel nucleation or ion implantation methods.

Object detection frameworks are available with significant numbers and diverse options, resulting in a challenge for researchers and practitioners to choose the most suitable one for their project. Incompatibility can lead to the loss of a living donor's kidney, a significant outcome. To make the most of valuable compatible donations, deciding on accepting incompatible ones becomes a crucial choice. In previous studies, this decision-making process has been modeled using Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), but only taking into account compatible exchanges. Our novel approach incorporates both compatible and incompatible decisions in an extended MDP model, where the state is defined by compatible information alone. By treating the acceptance of incompatible cases as a function of the current state, our approach simplifies the complex model and aids in understanding the problem at hand. Numerical experiments demonstrate that making the decision based on the current state leads to significant gains in the expected number of transplants made. Our results further reveal that the ideal policy of accepting certain incompatible cases can be characterized by an option set. A similar option set appears in the original model, indicating that the current approach of making decisions may lead to unnecessary MDP state variations and, consequently, an overestimation of the current model's expected number of transplants made.

This paper sets the stage for more accurate and unbiased NLP that avoids the risks of extreme language polarisation.

A major challenge in modeling fluid dynamics is Rayleigh-Bénard instability, which occurs when a fluid layer is heated from below and cools from above, eventually leading to the development of convection rolls. Traditionally, this problem has been addressed by creating detailed mathematical models and conducting laboratory experiments, but these methods are time-consuming and costly. Our research presents a novel approach that utilizes an machine learning algorithm called Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to accurately simulate and predict the behavior of a heated fluid layer. By combining this algorithm with numerical differentiation techniques, we were able to successfully reproduce the characteristic "roll cells" that form during the instability phase and accurately estimate the critical point at which the instability occurs. Our findings show that with moderate training, our neural network model can accurately estimate the instability threshold, although some adjustments may be necessary to fully capture the spatial aspects of the instability. Overall, this research highlights the potential of using PINNs as a powerful tool for solving complex fluid dynamics problems, providing an efficient and accurate method for solving the underlying advection-diffusion equation.

This paper describes the implementation of PDF fitting within the PyPDF framework, beginning with an overview of the DGLAP evolution method and subsequent presentation of various fitting techniques at leading order, NLO, and higher orders. This research introduces variance reduction techniques through experience replay (VRER) for enhancing the stability of policy gradient methods in deep reinforcement learning. We put forward a novel PPIR (Periodic Experience Replay) training strategy to address the issue of limited data efficiency caused by the use of experience replay in policy gradient networks. Our studies indicate that VRER methods consistently outperform traditional policy gradient approaches that rely on single-step dynamics, demonstrating improved performance and convergence characteristics. Moreover, our results reveal that increasing the size of the experience pool can lead to significant gains in performance. We also present two techniques to mitigate the absolute minimum fidelity problem and restore data efficiency while maintaining the benefits of VRER. Our findings provide a new perspective for exploring the theoretical underpinnings and limitations of policy gradient methods.

The development of the code MG-GLAM is described, which combines the features of the general-purpose code GLAM and the large-scale N-body code GLAM-SunGa. MediaWiki, the open-source wiki platform behind Wikipedia, is used to publish our manuscripts on ArXiv and develop our software tools, forming an integral part of our research process. The objective of this study is to develop a theoretical model that accurately represents the linear interaction between the velocity and temperature fluctuations in a turbulent flame. This is done by applying a stochastic approach to a single-point Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations. Using the Flame Propagation Speed (FPS) model, the probability distribution of the filter function is approximated, and the probability distribution of the local state is modeled as delta-function. The result of this approach is that closure assumptions for the stochastic model of the local state are obtained. The validity of this model is tested through direct numerical simulation of methane-air combustion at a moderate mass flux through a circular pipe with sudden expansion and through contraction. The stochastic model accurately predicts interaction between velocity and temperature fluctuations in the linear interaction region and the transition to fully developed turbulence after the flow reattachment. The Flame Progress Variable (FPV) model was also compared to the FPS model and found that the FPV model does not accurately represent the local state. The model that best fits the linear interaction framework is the FPS model with the probability distribution of the local state modeled as the delta-function. This is done by applying the stochastic approach to the single-point Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations and using the Flame Progress Variable (FPV) model. We consider a scenario with an ultralight dark matter candidate that interacts very weakly with neutrinos, creating a potential mechanism for neutrino mass origin. The behavior of the early Universe in this case is significantly influenced by this interaction, leading to possible self-acceleration or the development of a matter component. However, for our proposed ideas to align with the observed properties of the Cosmic Microwave Background and large scale structure, the density of dark matter must reach a level where radiation domination ensues. If the ultralight dark matter is coupled to sterile neutrinos, cosmic structure formation imposes constraints on its parameters. If instead it interacts with active neutrinos, it can result in either an over-abundance of matter in our scenario or neutrino masses in disagreement with experimental data, respectively. Thus, in order for this theory to be plausible, it calls for an additional mechanism that can produce sufficient amounts of dark matter in the early Universe or modify the expansion rate during radiation domination.

A novel nonlocal gravitational theory is developed by us, based on a reorganization of the Einstein-Hilbert action that involves a exponential factor and a derivative operator that can be applied multiple times. This approach leads to an innovative relationship between the gravity's stress-energy tensor and the matter's stress-energy tensor, which is influenced by the theory's two key parameters, the inverse mass squared and an infinite dimension parameter. By adjusting these parameters appropriately, the nonlocal gravitational model returns to the general theory of relativity. Furthermore, the newly proposed relationship enables recovery of key results from nonlocal gravity models that contain an exponential factor, without the risk of encountering singularities due to infinite dimensions. This is particularly beneficial for addressing issues related to perturbations around de Sitter spacetime and avoiding problems with infinite powers of Hubble parameter.

Understanding the relationship between snRNA and protein R in complex trait genetics is essential, particularly in the intermediate stage. Although previous studies have explored the connection between phenotype-associated SNPs and functional elements in snRNA or protein R for specific traits, a comprehensive analysis of the primary driver - whether it be gene expression, protein sequence, or other factors in the intermediate stage between genotype and phenotype, across the genetic landscape of different associated SNPs and species with varying phenotypic complexities - has not been conducted. Using latent variable analysis, a significant relationship between the associated SNPs in gene expression, snRNA, and protein R was found in over hundred human species traits, with approximately seventy percent of SNPs associated with a complex trait being linked to the protein R, with the link being more pronounced in morphological or physiological traits. A significant relationship between the associated SNPs and gene expression was also found in about thirty percent of the cases, with a stronger connection in traits involving cell type or location. A LVA model that included random effects and carried out cross-validation with parameters regulated by variance significantly improved, in contrast to a model without these components.

The discovery of the 2018 REissA 1 transient, initially mistaken for a neutron star low mass X-ray binary, highlights the need for precise classifications of such events. Researchers have been studying the minimum conditions for hydrogen burning in these objects as a way to differentiate between the largest brown dwarfs and the smallest stars. However, previous studies made this analysis with simple spherical assumptions. Our research pushes the boundary by considering the effects of angular momentum in a brown dwarf or stellar object that has surpassed the limit for hydrogen burning. Using the "effective angular momentum threshold" concept, our study calculates the impact of spinning at speeds below and above this threshold on the critical curves that define the minimum conditions for hydrogen burning. Our calculations take into account the influence of angular momentum on the critical curves, which in turn depends on the direction of the spin. Our calculations indicate that when an object spins slower than this threshold, the minimum temperature required for hydrogen burning rises, while the opposite is true when the spin exceeds this threshold. As angular speed increases, the difference in angular speed also increases, resulting in differences that can reach up to 5 K for objects with 0.06 solar masses. The differences in rotation speed also affect the required hydrogen burning temperature, affecting the long-term cooling of sub-stellar objects and potentially the difference between the largest brown dwarfs and the smallest stars.

We examine the problem of creating a planar diagram for 2-WCG graphs, which are graph types that are close to planar representations. Our research also considers a more basic version of the problem with a ham-sandwich separator and achieves an arrangement with a simple cycle separating the graph's components, again through strategic conversion of vertices into "split" points.

We examine the power series series field, denoted as K[[X]], where K represents a field and X is a variable, in relation to the residue map that associates each series with its initial coefficient. In dynamic environments where challenges vary significantly, simpler problems can be overlooked by agents, leading to inefficiencies that may have widespread consequences. To address this issue, we developed a model where the difficulty levels of problems are spread unevenly, forcing at least two agents to cooperate in order to thrive. We examined how this distribution affects the strategies of agents with differing levels of inaccuracy. Our research reveals that agents are likely to neglect the easier problems and focus on the harder ones, which can lead to notable inefficiencies in solving problems within a certain difficulty range. Our model also highlights the impact of differences in accuracy among the agents, showing that they may focus on problems with higher difficulty levels than if they had identical accuracy. Our findings highlight the importance of understanding difficulty distributions and exploring nonobvious regions of problems, which can be applied to various fields, from psychology to space exploration.

The vulnerability of VFL privacy has attracted considerable interest in recent years, primarily due to collaborative learning applications involving sensitive data. Our laboratory conducted a comprehensive investigation into vulnerabilities under the shared sample learning protocol, revealing that even basic algorithms are susceptible to membership attacks. Specifically, we found that even single-person membership attacks are feasible, whereas previously reported findings necessitated at least three colluding participants. The extent of these attacks varies based on the relationship between learning and test sets but generally achieves high precision and recall. Furthermore, we observed that algorithms employing cryptographic techniques are also vulnerable and our precision and recall results did not significantly change in response to increasing dataset sizes. Similarly, our research indicated that surface level privacy protection offers no defense against membership attacks with comparable results. Ultimately, our algorithm susceptibility findings suggest that the underlying VFL privacy issues are more widespread than previously assumed and encompass both traditional and contemporary validation algorithms.

We introduce a novel kernel approximation method called Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), which optimizes the efficiency of RFF by significantly reducing the dimension of features while maintaining high prediction accuracy. RFF maps data points using a specific set of features derived from cosine transformations and random frequencies, enabling the use of kernel methods for non-linear separable tasks. However, this approach can be computationally expensive for large datasets. In contrast, PRFF utilizes the principle of low density parity checks to generate more compact features from the RFF framework. Our experimental evaluations across multiple kernel methods and datasets demonstrate that PRFF achieves nearly identical prediction performance to RFF, even with a substantially reduced feature set (20-50 times smaller).

This paper conducts an in-depth examination of the Cartesian Decomposition problem, a difficult instance of the Orbit Equivalence problem. We start by resolving it for regular group actions and then move on to prove that the Cartesian Decomposition problem is undecidable for actions of free groups of rank 2 that are equipped with word metrics, in collaboration with S. Donati. Additionally, we provide a method to identify a specific configuration in the Cartesian decompositions of actions with the same configuration space and fundamental domains, given that they are equipped with the same Weyl chambers.

This research proves that in any given dimension (for a specific threshold), the constant M\"obius scalar curvature can be achieved as the highest possible value for the range of achievable values for the set of all compact hypersurfaces that can be conformally flat and are embedded in n-dimensional space. Achieving this peak is possible only when a (n-1)-dimensional sphere is embedded in the constant M\"obius scalar curvature space of dimension n. These conclusions are supported by a key lemma regarding embedded (n-1)-spheres with induced M\"obius scalar curvature for any dimension.

This research paper introduces a novel Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique (GAST) designed to enhance efficiency in wireless Power Information Theory (SWIPT) systems where simultaneous information and power are being transmitted. We investigate an ORC-based SWIPT system where a base station with multiple antennas transmits data and energy to an informed user with several antennas, by formulating an optimization problem that aims to minimize the decoding time at the user's end, while ensuring adequate information and power transmission rates, as well as accounting for beamformer norm constraints and antenna-switching efficiency. We demonstrate that by leveraging an informed user's perfect channel knowledge, an optimal pattern can be identified to reduce the decoding delay, and we employ a coordinate descent method to solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem. We also establish that traditional Antenna-Switching Techniques represent particular instances of our Generalized model. We further examine the absence of SWIPT over certain frequency bands, leading to an entirely convex problem that can be resolved using standard optimization solvers. We then extend our investigation to include an ideal processor at the user's end, and ultimately, we gather empirical evidence of the practical feasibility of GAST from numerical results.

We investigate the process of full random-metric-hub fragmentation that arises from the removal of a single node within complex networks. Our study focuses on scale-free networks specifically, and we analyze how other nodes become unconnected as a result of the one node's complete removal. Our theoretical framework employs a percolation-like approach combined with an averaging strategy, which we validate through numerical simulations. Furthermore, we explore the impact of the network's size, connection size distribution, and distance distribution on the unconnected nodes. Additionally, we utilize our method to efficiently estimate the results of the removal of random nodes, and we utilize this strategy to examine the effects of the "SIR" infection spread caused by the one node's removal. Our findings from this study also have implications for assessing the stability of complex networks.

A theoretical design for a sensitivity improvement instrument called a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer is presented as an alternative to conventional interferometric systems. The proposed design incorporates dynamic movement into a fiber-optic Sagnac interferometer loop to leverage moving medium sensitivity gains and is capable of enhancing the photon path length by reversing the return trajectory of light. Analytical and numerical analyses of this system are conducted to evaluate its linearity, line rate, phasor behavior, and sensitivity to rotation, revealing significant line-rate limitations but also substantial improvements in length control. The research also explores the potential use of this design in applications requiring high precision, such as inertial navigation n-eeds and space-based N-body simulations orbitocalculations.

The NOVR-XL (Neighbour Opportunity Variable-Retry for Extreme-scale systems) random access (RA) protocol has been developed to significantly enhance random access performance in extreme-large Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) systems. This protocol leverages the opportunity created by extreme-scale networks to utilise overheard information from neighbouring cells. NOVR-XL is adaptable and can modify its behaviour based on the size of the backlogged queue. It also modifies the number of contention resolution (CR) opportunities by observing the performance in neighbouring cells. A theoretical analysis of the protocol is conducted and its performance is compared with existing solutions. The results of simulation studies are presented for extreme-large networks.

A new astrophysical simulation methodology combines substructure modeling and hydrodynamics to model a protoplanetary disk. This model incorporates multiple enhancement factors, including waves, gaps, surface brightness variations, and vertical disk features, and is capable of modeling low-mass planet formation up to the point where planets become embedded within the disk midplane. Initial numerical experiments use "spikes" and "gaps" to gradually migrate embedded planetesimals and migrate them to the disk midplane with minimal radial displacement or additional mass, as seen in planetary disk imagery. These results offer valuable insights for future high-resolution numerical simulations and suggest possible explanations for bright features observed in planetary disk features.

Our research has developed a variant of the BigApple$^\text{2014}$ relativistic mean-field model for nuclei, by modifying its energy density functional to include specific components. By adjusting these components, we have increased the proton number of nuclei that can be accurately reproduced without losing agreement with nuclear data. When reparameterized, this functional demonstrates robust performance in various calculations, including low-energy nuclear excitation and nuclear matter properties, and even allows us to accurately simulate the equation of state required to explain results from a gravitational wave detection event, known as GW170817.

The efficiency of the commonly used Mølmer-Sørensen entanglement gate in ion traps is significantly influenced by its design, particularly in scenarios where measurement feedback plays a role or when entanglement is accumulated over time. Our in-depth analysis of the MS gate reveals novel insights, uncovering that non-oscillatory gate designs inevitably accumulate more entanglement than their oscillatory counterparts, regardless of external noise influences. Variations in laser parameters influence near-gate entanglement accumulation but not the overall trend, indicating that fundamental MS gate dynamics consistently drive average entanglement growth. However, noise characteristics can dictate variations in accumulated entanglement, particularly low-frequency noise that plays a more significant role in continuous, feedback-driven entanglement accumulation. Findings from our research provide instructive insights for experimental design and highlight the necessity of carefully selecting and varying the entanglement accumulation drive to minimize noise-induced variations in accumulated entanglement.

We have conducted a comprehensive investigation of the chemical compound GaCu3(OH)6Cl2, which previously showed susceptibility to magnetic fields and structural changes at its phase transition temperature. Our research reveals that structurally, this compound belongs to the chlorohydroxide family, and it can be seen as derived from the parent compound LCu3(OH)6Cl2 by substituting Ga for Cu at specific crystallographic sites. Notably, GaCu3(OH)6Cl2 exhibits a very narrow band structure, consisting of nearly equivalent s and p copper orbitals near its Fermi level. Due to its unique square lattice configuration with strong in-plane bonding and weak perpendicular offset, this material has the potential to display contradictory characteristics of 2D dirac electrons and complex quantum many-body physics. Our findings are supported by high-quality X-ray scattering data, demonstrating the validity of our modeling approach.

Simply integrating an $N$-gram model with a neural language model yields a neural component that is analogous to an $N$-gram model and a traditional component that is analogous to a neural network, which has been found to improve performance in various language tasks, including machine translation and text summarization. However, existing research on this topic has relied on hand-crafted features or domain-specific techniques. In this study, we investigate the underlying principles of this approach by exploring the combination of $n$-grams and neural models in machine translation. Without using any task-specific techniques or additional features, we developed various models of the $n$-gram + neural model type and trained them according to the standard training procedure. These models were evaluated on multiple translation tasks, including English-Chinese and Farsi. Our results show that automatic $n$-gram model selection can yield performance gains, leading to better results with a smaller $n$-gram model. Additionally, we found that training an $n$-gram model on back-translated data can further enhance performance, particularly in low-resource settings. Our research also reveals that combining a automatic selected $n$-gram model with neural models trained with back-translated data yields the best results.

This paper presents a new deep learning network called SADRNet, which utilizes a self-aligned dual face regression method to reconstruct faces from images showing different angles. The network automatically separates features that change with angles and those that do not, without any manual input. It does this by using two alignment modules and two regression modules in its U-Net architecture. The modules are designed to extract features that do and do not change with angles, and then combine them to recreate the face at any given angle. Experimental results show significant improvements in accuracy compared to other methods, with a 7.195 point gain in overall performance, and also demonstrate real-world applicability.

This work presents a method for improving character recognition accuracy using a corrector based on n-grams, with the goal of testing its effectiveness in a real-world application such as vote counting in optical character recognition systems. To achieve this, we first configure a corrector that accounts for adjacent character swaps, then compare the performance of this corrector with a basic one in processing a set of highly erroneous texts produced by a character recognition system with a high error rate. By analyzing the impact of the corrector on classification results, we demonstrate that this method can significantly improve accuracy in scenarios where precise results are critical.

A challenge with models that have more parameters than data points and time-varying data, especially when the number of parameters is very large compared to the number of observations, remains unclear on how to effectively handle dependent variables that change over time in infinite-dimensional spaces. To address this issue, this research conducts a theoretical analysis of non-stationary time series data using an innovative combination of methods, specifically the linear time-varying operator regularized by a nuclear norm. Moreover, we develop an algorithm based on alternating minimization to efficiently find parameter operator estimates, and our research reveals that under certain conditions, our method outperforms simple regression models that ignore time dependence. Ultimately, numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and reveal its capacity to handle complex, non-stationary data patterns.

The paper examines the implications of using a utility function in energy systems with carbon pricing and pricing volatility for future policy-making. It finds that volatility in carbon prices encourages the use of storage resources, even when accounting for risk-averse behavior. However, when analyzing the impact of a risk-averse storage resource, it is discovered that it may not always be more conservative than one with quadratic cost functions, which can result in it actually emitting more CO2 in certain conditions. Consequently, policies that consider future risk and replace carbon prices with a range could be ineffective when applied to storage resources. It is also noted that the results may vary depending on the type of storage resource, which implies that future policy decisions should be tailored to specific resources. It is recommended that further research be conducted with more diverse risk functions and storage resources that consider both energy storage and generation.

A key component in the Mars atmosphere circulation pattern is baroclinic storms, which feature strong temperature variations horizontal to the flow and are well-documented since the 1999 global dust season. During this period, the atmosphere was heavily clouded seasonally, likely triggering the planet-wide circulation disruption. Comparable effects have been predicted for dust seasons on Titan. We examined how the atmosphere would respond to various levels of cloud coverage during a specific period: northern winter in a Mars-like atmosphere and a Earth-like atmosphere subject to seasonal lake coverage. Under certain conditions, the atmosphere could experience sudden changes in temperature gradients, leading to surface winds that reversed direction and a buildup of aerosols near the poles. The baroclinic storms observed in the Mars atmosphere during the 1999 global dust season match well with model predictions, notably the reversal of surface jets and the disruption of gravity waves in the upper atmosphere. The model also produced sound-like variations in upper atmospheric densities and a dust season lasting one Earth year is too brief to sustain a Earth-like atmosphere. The study suggests that atmospheric thickening would require years lasting hundreds of Earth years, as seen in the Titan atmosphere.

The effectiveness of a specific two-qubit gate, known as the exchange interaction between two adjacent phosphorus donor atoms in silicon, is dependent on their separation distance. While precise control over this interaction is possible, its high sensitivity to slight variations in placement makes real-time adjustment necessary. This study demonstrates the implementation of a feedback loop that responds to a response signal from a Ramsey experiment, resulting in a measurable response that reflects the two-qubit gate's effectiveness. By utilizing this response as feedback, the response magnitude is minimized, indicating excellent effectiveness of the gate. These results are demonstrated with silicon-mosfets at low temperatures, where the donor atoms are placed 3.5 nanometers below the surface, allowing for real-time control over the exchange interaction through electric fields. This is evident from the ability to tune the gate more than five orders of magnitude, with a bandwidth exceeding one kilohertz. These results indicate that a response similar to what has been demonstrated can be used for a robust implementation of quantum error correction algorithms for two qubits.

Our research reveals that resistance fluctuations near the zero Landau level in large-scale samples exhibit distinct features. Specifically, we found that the period, width, and behavior of these oscillations change with sample size. In smaller samples, the oscillations are caused by electron scattering between opposite spins within the zero Landau level. As samples become larger, scattering between opposite spins gives way to processes involving three or more particles. This shift is evident in the  $\hbar\omega_c$ displacement of the oscillation peak and its gradual widening. Moreover, we discovered that adding the components of the Dingle function that traditionally describe the amplitude of the Su Shubnikov de Haas and zero-field effects fails to capture the data, necessitating the inclusion of a third parameter in our fitting function. This third parameter accounts for processes that involve three or more particles.

In rapidly evolving Time Division Duplex (TDD) networks, an innovative solution for optimizing both resource allocation and scheduling along with adaptive configuration is presented. A two-phase approach is proposed to address this issue. Initially, a decentralized method for balancing uplink and downlink usage is presented. This method involves estimating key parameters, allocating time periods for transmission, and evaluating performance. Secondly, an optimized method for routing is presented that utilizes key parameters to balance allocation between training and data transmission. Key performance indicators such as sum-rate and energy efficiency are considered in this research. Mathematical models and simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solution in achieving significant improvements in system efficiency.

We present a novel architecture known as a Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN), which integrates Hamiltonian dynamics into the framework of Neural Networks. 
HNN utilizes a LSTM-based learning component and a Hamiltonian-based component derived from a neural network, allowing it to efficiently model symmetries and translational invariances while capturing complex patterns. 
Our evaluation shows the HNN achieves superior results compared to the LSTM-based learning component alone, particularly when dealing with tasks involving the MNIST dataset. 
Furthermore our HNN framework reveals insights into Hamiltonian dynamics by examining gradients of the Hamiltonian with respect to phase space variables, which enables us to detect and visualize symmetries and patterns. 
Our study demonstrates the HNN achieves excellent performance and provides a framework to analyze and visualize the underlying symmetries and patterns of data.

In rapidly evolving environments where machine learning models are constantly changing, ensuring model reliability has become a significant challenge. Researchers are exploring cooperative solutions using multiple agents to maintain model accuracy and trustworthiness. We propose an innovative framework consisting of several specialized agents that collaborate through both task division and sharing to elevate the performance of machine learning models. Evaluations using two case studies on dynamic classification and long-short term memory models show that our proposed system outperforms singular agent setups and significantly improves model accuracy and trust score with further optimization. By breaking down complex research problems, we achieve notable reductions in training time while achieving comparable results.

To reach high performance levels in modern NLP tasks using deep learning, these models need a substantial amount of training data. The effectiveness of data augmentation has been proven across various NLP applications, such as word embeddings, semantic role labeling, machine translation, and text classification. Our approach takes inspiration from successful data augmentation methods and employs semantic text similarity to manually expand labeled texts with semantically similar variants. These augmented data points are used for retraining models to evaluate their improved performance over the original dataset alone, ETL scripts and container configurations for the associated environment are included. Our primary contribution is a method for efficiently augmenting labeled text classes for text classification tasks through controlled data augmentation. Our experiments show that E2E data augmentation methodologies can yield significant improvements over their unaugmented counterparts, although the most gains were not overwhelmingly large.

The rapidly evolving natural language understanding by large language models poses a challenge in accurately managing structured data within relational databases when dealing with text-based queries. This project presents a novel, modular framework called SParC, which breaks down the execution accuracy, data fulfillment, and result verification processes, all significantly enhanced by a dedicated mechanism that leverages reverse tracing to ensure results' correctness. What sets SParC apart is its four reverse tracing modules, which analyze the result format, fill in missing data, and verify the query execution by going backwards from the result to the original query. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we developed a prototype based on SParC and pre-trained it on a diverse dataset of 2,000 randomly selected questions from the Spider training set paired with their corresponding database contents. When compared to state-of-the-art methods, execution accuracy was found to be superior without access to database contents and outperformed existing methods when access was granted. Additionally, individual components of our system were found to be effective, with the addition of reverse tracing mechanisms boosting execution accuracy by 5.3 percent, as well as 21.0 percent and 2.0 percent, as shown in results across the development, test-long, and test-short sets respectively. These findings highlight the efficacy of our proposed framework, which provides a robust foundation for future research in data management systems.

In graph-based machine learning models, ensuring the privacy of individuals whose data points are interconnected poses a significant challenge, as this interconnectivity complicates the computation of data dependencies. As a result, researchers have been exploring the potential of leveraging graph structures to enhance efficiency while maintaining data privacy. However, when graph-based learning algorithms are used, it remains unclear how to effectively balance privacy preservation with the ability to utilize graph structure information. This paper presents a novel graph structure privacy mechanism that leverages graph information to create efficient data representations, as well as theoretical analysis of its impact on learning performance. Furthermore, the proposed method is applied to develop an optimized graph neural network model that can utilize privacy-preserving graph information to improve learning performance. The model demonstrates its effectiveness and versatility through experimental results on various classification tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and semi-supervised learning.

A comprehensive assessment of the data anticipated from the Euclid mission is conducted across various fields of astronomy, including cosmological research, structure formation, galaxy research, transients, asteroids, comets, and extragalactic and extraterrestrial studies, as well as areas that will exploit the vast amount of data collected. Specific galaxy surveys, based on new extragalactic galaxy data, are outlined for the photometric investigation using Euclid and the combined datasets it will produce, while extragalactic and extraterrestrial studies primarily focus on comprehensive coverage provided by Euclid. The report also delves into the potential of machine learning algorithms to develop across galaxies, transients, asteroids, and comets studies, as well as extragalactic and extraterrestrial research, leveraging the extensive data Euclid will generate.

By incorporating the effects of composite observables, this approach combines hydrodynamic models with L\'{e}vy area terms generated through stochastic components to reproduce the full Kadanovskaya-Baym equations for one-particle properties. The resulting model is applied to simulate the properties of a one-particle distribution in a two-dimensional quantum field during the radiation process following a heavy ion collision. The results obtained from this simulation are identical to those achieved through fully relativistic Monte Carlo simulations for L\'{e}vy areas of current and position. However, for longer times and larger charges, quantum backreaction effects are evident and the one-particle distribution deviates from both fully self-consistent Monte Carlo and hydrodynamic calculations.

We establish the quenched large deviation principle for sequences of letters in a stationary and ergodic renewal process, with rates determined by the probability of letter sequences, demonstrating its convergence for rare events. Our analysis also reveals the relationship between the LDP tail exponents and the tail behavior of the process's intervals between repeated letters. Furthermore, we identify the additivity of the LDP rates in constructions that involve the independent combination of renewal processes. By employing the quenched LDP, we derive the tail exponents for random walks built on random graphs where edge lengths follow random distributions, and we obtain bounds on the tail probabilities for sums of i.i.d. random walks defined on edge lengths, which include the "random climber" model.
