This paper presents a novel algorithm for Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO) that leverages an end-to-end trained optical flow model along with traditional state, feature point, and residual measurements. The primary distinction between our approach and conventional VIO methods lies in the type of measurement data employed. Unlike other works that integrate various optimization techniques for flow estimation to enhance accuracy, we develop a sophisticated combination of optimization methods and fuse multiple measurement types to compensate for the imperfections of the pure end-to-end VIO solution. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach yields a 22% improvement in terminal residue for the SOD dataset vis-à-vis the original end-to-end solution, with comparable computational costs and memory usage.

We investigate higher-order Weyl semimetals in three dimensions, exploring their rich topological properties and robust edge states that appear in both time-reversal and charge-conjugation breaking systems. In our study, we analyze several theoretical models, revealing various forms of topological invariants that characterize higher-order topology, including a new, previously unexplored aspect of wire-like Topological Charge pumping based on dynamic $ \mathbf{K} $-matrix topology. Our theoretical framework also incorporates a new classification system for higher-order Weyl semimetals, categorized by the behavior of Fermi arcs at the boundaries of their Topological charge. We establish the existence of characteristic surface states, referred to as "crops," in certain high-order Weyl semimetals, which we identify through the polarization charge and K-matrix topology. Our research includes the re-examination of previous high-order Weyl semimetals and the proposal of several new models, such as the $ \mathbf{D}^{2} $ SSH model, exhibiting rich higher-order topology in time-crystalline systems. Our findings hold relevance for various material systems, as we discuss the possibility of realising high-order Weyl semimetallic phases in the $ \mathbf{PbTa_2S_6} $ family of materials.

This study presents a novel approach to Data Completion that accounts for incomplete measurements on the boundary of a specific region. The method involves selecting a computational grid and formulating the data completion problem as an optimization task that can be efficiently solved using high-order numerical techniques. The absolute value gradient term in the optimization functional provides regularisation and enables the use of edge finite elements, which accurately interpolate missing data on the given domain. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this method through various numerical experiments with 2D simulations.

We introduce a novel application of knowledge distillation for natural language knowledge amalgamation, leveraging KNN for task adaptation. Our approach utilizes implicit bias exploitation through representative sampling of salient training samples, focusing on the selection mechanism for salience. We assess two distinct frameworks: a baseline based on neighbor importance and an innovative method that ranks neighbors based on class probability. These models were tested on various classes within the multi-class Textual Entailment MNLI dataset, with a teacher model trained using the same data as the student model to ensure fair comparison. Our experiments with dynamic activation indicate that our approach effectively identifies critical neighbors, deactivating 99% of neighbors in average, while enhancing the performance of a fully active model. Our approach is implemented in The Distiller repository.

Using the example of $N=11$, we explore the set of quartic extensions of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ where the elliptic curve $34161a1$ acquires an elliptic subcurve over an ordered field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$, given that it does not increase in rank. For a specific isotropic S4 quartic extension, the curve becomes rigid and thus cannot gain rank. There are two non-isomorphic extensions that allow the curve to gain rank by one.

Quantum quenches in many-body systems lead to valuable insights regarding the dynamics of nonequilibrium dynamics and thermodynamics. Our research focuses on the connection between the dynamics of temperature changes and the production of irreversible entropy during external-driven dynamics. By employing the Matsubara nonequilibrium action, we establish a direct link between the production of irreversible entropy and the work performed during external-driven dynamics. Our analysis utilizes the worldline quantum Monte Carlo (WMQMC) method to study the dynamics of temperature and the production of irreversible entropy. By comparing our findings with the Gross-Pitaevskii and Stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii equations, we find consistent results andWMQMC data for real-time dynamics of temperature and irreversible entropy production. We present presentations of the production of irreversible entropy in relation to the work done and the mean-field dynamics of temperature and irreversible entropy.

We present an alternative perspective on the time at which a quantum system's non-unitary evolution begins to exhibit unitary behavior, positing that the system and its environment must first be describable as a collection of quasi-particles before the evolution can be modeled as a unitary process. Our primary finding is that time-twirling the initial system-environment state at the moment non-unitary dynamics start is equivalent to preparing a state where the information quantum fidelity reaches a maximum, a property that can be met in various models of dissipative dynamics. Multiple models of non-unitary dynamics are then shown to be describable as unitary interactions between the system and the environment starting from a system-environment state that maximizes information quantum fidelity.

This research paper introduces regular simplexes with unique interpolation properties. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any set of $d$ distinct points within a high-dimensional unit cube, there exists a nondegenerate regular simplex that contains these points on its surface. Our findings also imply that the maximum dimension for a simplectic graph in a unit cube follows the condition $d < 2^{\tau(n)},$ where $\tau(n)$ represents the number of ones in the binary notation of $n$. Our results are applicable, for instance, to determine the dimension of the unit cube with $1024$ vertices that can support a regular simplex with $45$ vertices on its surface.

Silicon wafers were processed using the EOE technique and subsequently etched to produce surfaces with minimal or no residual carrier concentration. In etched silicon (ES), found in androgen receptor cancer therapy applications, the etched surfaces exhibit a wide range of carrier concentrations. To better understand the physical characteristics of these surfaces, measurements of carrier concentration, surface microstructure, and surface roughness were conducted on both EOE and ES samples across various degrees of carrier concentration reduction. In contrast to EOE samples, ES surfaces displayed significant crystalline features and higher carrier concentrations. In particular, regions with the highest carrier concentrations, which make up the majority of ES samples, exhibited a specific pattern of dislocation loops with edge character. These patterns matched those observed in heavily doped silicon that has been annealed at high temperatures. Moreover, the carrier concentration profiles of the highest-concentration regions resembled the profiles seen in high-resistivity silicon wafers that have been diffused at high temperatures to create super ohmic contact surfaces. These findings have important implications for creating surfaces with very low carrier concentration required in androgen receptor cancer therapy applications. In particular, the similar features of the highest-concentration regions suggest that surface cleaning techniques that involve high-temperature treatments may be less effective in lowering the carrier concentration in certain ES samples.

Far from equilibrium systems, including our planet in the future, may experience significant atmospheric evolution driven by material recycling between a planet's interior and surface. To comprehend such scenarios fully, it is crucial to consider both its surface and interior dynamics. Here, we employ a coupled climate-convective model to examine the long-term interaction between the atmosphere and interior of a water-rich planet with an extensive ocean, using an Earth-like planet that enters a runaway state as an example. In this model, we examine how the atmosphere and interior cycle together by modeling how the planet's rotation rate, albedo, and heat transport influence each other. When our model planet enters a moist greenhouse state, both its surface temperature and rotation rate begin to accelerate, but eventually, significant amounts of water are lost to space and melting rock absorbs energy from its interior, leaving our model planet with a fast rotation rate, high temperature, and thin atmosphere - a state that could be detected by missions like TRAPPIST-1.

In this paper, we outline methods for modeling multivariate point processes using the nonlinear Hawkes process model. A general framework is introduced that encompasses various Hawkes process models and estimation techniques. We analyze models based on Volterra series and compare their performance through a case study using transaction data from the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

Research into polarization rotation using plasma plates is being revived for next-generation high-energy gamma-ray telescopes like eST. To effectively achieve this, a significant thickness is necessary for the plasma plate, with requirements that can be met by density breakdown in some cases, or which may be circumvented through plasma plates located in very high-strength magnetic fields, up to 10^4 Gauss. We examine plasma plate properties that exist in such fields, focusing on Faraday rotation efficiency, plate thickness, and the relationship between dispersion and plate properties. A key aspect involves modeling how plasma plates must be modeled anisotropically, similar to how the magnetosphere of pulsars is modeled. Our model shows that the necessary plate thickness increases with the square of the electron density and is directly proportional to the magnetic field strength. Our model is illustrated with examples that consider the plasma plate requirements for the eST mission.

We investigated the Higgs sector within the theory that expands upon the Standard Model, specifically focusing on a type-II two-Higgs doublet model, and explored the sources of both radiative and direct generation of the tau electric dipole moment. By analyzing possible contributions, we determined the ranges for radiative and direct generation of this moment, which are $10^{-20} e\cdot cm \leqq \sigma_{10^{-19}}\leqq 10^{-2} e\cdot cm$ and $10^{-26} e\cdot cm \leqq \sigma_{10^{-19}}\leqq 10^{-4} e\cdot cm$, respectively. We also identified the key parameters influencing the size of this moment and, utilizing current data from LHC and other experiments, we established constraints on its magnitude, which are $\sigma_{10^{-20}} \leqq 0.17$ and $\sigma_{10^{-17}} \leqq 0.8$, as measured by the electric dipole moment of the tau particle.

This paper investigates rank error correction codes, comparing them to their symbol-based correction equivalents. We investigate the relationship between their error correction capabilities, revealing a distinct behavior for rates under 1/2 and rates over 1/2. Additionally, we identify precise conditions where the rank code outperforms the symbol code, and provide a method for constructing codes that satisfy these conditions.

We investigate the operator product expansion (OPE) blocks of conserved current fields along geodesic paths in a conformal field theory (CFT$_2$) and express these blocks using geodesic operators in the corresponding anti-de Sitter space (AdS$_2$). Our analysis reveals that current OPE blocks maintain their representation when transitioning from a geodesic in CFT$_2$ to one in AdS$_2$, unlike scalar fields which modify their form. Notably, AdS$_3$ geodesic operators do not appear in the expansion of current OPE blocks along geodesic paths. Our findings could have significant implications for understanding the bulk dual of the Fermi surface through the "smearing" method.

In 1991, Gelfand and MacPherson introduced the concept of the long complex of the Grassmannian, which was found to be deeply related to the free differential Lie algebra of a certain combinatorial structure. This paper aims to demonstrate that the homology of the long complex is equivalent to the homology of the free differential Lie algebra, providing a precise characterization: H_n(C_long(G(r,n))) is equal to direct sum from k=2 to n of T_r(K_n^k), where T_r denotes the exterior product with itself r times. As a result, this finding implies that the long complex of the Grassmannian, C_long(G(r,n)), when subjected to its natural grading, has the property of being weakly free when r is odd, and nearly free when r is even.

Ni/Fe ratios in explosive events, particularly supernovae and kilonovae, can vary widely due to differences in their physical conditions. These properties are heavily influenced by factors that also affect the Ti/Si ratios. Observing Ni/Fe and Ti/Si ratios allows for an in-depth examination of a supernova's early stages. However, Ni/Fe ratios in SN~2020jfo may not reflect the core conditions as the element iron is dominated by self-absorption, which can fully remove iron lines but not those of nickel because of its weaker presence. This results in an overestimation of Ni/Fe ratios in SN~2020jfo, which could be as high as 2.5 times the current value. Due to this, we recommend focusing on Ti/Si ratios in SN~2020jfo, which are more reliable for research purposes. If we assume the iron self-absorption behaves similarly in SN~2020jfo and CN~2018hg, then the overestimation of Ni/Fe ratios in CN~2018hg is even more pronounced. This is because the iron content is likely higher in CN~2018hg than in SN~2020jfo, which has a weaker absorption band. Consequently, Ni/FE ratios in CN~2018hg are at least 5 times higher than in SN~2020

This study investigates the identification of specific cross-shaped image segments resulting from point source observations via a lobster-eye optics system integrated into an X-ray telescope. We analyzed the azimuthal rotation angles of these cross segments in relation to the incident X-rays for various mirror cell configurations. The results demonstrate that the angle of rotation for each segment can be directly correlated to its corresponding mirror cell segment, thereby facilitating the pinpointing of degraded segments that may require removal. The methodology developed in this study was successfully applied to actual data, revealing predictable angles of rotation for all segments and validating the hypothesis that the outer segments exhibiting larger angles of rotation correspond to the most outward-facing mirror cell segments.

Utilizing a probability-related approach, specifically by applying Bayes' rule, this study develops a framework for solving equations that are completely nonlinear in a rigorous manner. The method known as 'level set Monte Carlo' combines previous deterministic approach of solving these equations by resolving their associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system with a novel, Riemann-based formulation. The key feature of this formulation is its representation of the solution surface within the equation's solution space. The Monte Carlo method then comes into play to manage the high-dimensional integrations necessary for a wide range of fully nonlinear functions. The benefits of this formulation are evident, including the efficient handling of high-dimensional cases and the creation of robust numerical solutions, even for equations that are completely nonlinear.

We conducted an $800^3$-particle-mesh cosmological simulation labeled 'lensing' with an initially low scalar perturbation amplitude ($f_0=0.1$) to test the hypothesis that dark matter halos of the lensing category can be modeled without considering the effects of gravitational discontinuities. We analyzed halos with a mass range of $10^{11}-10^{12} h^{-2}M_{\odot}$ and found that the density-only model incorrectly predicts halo mass concentrations by a factor of 2--4, while the halo formation time discrepancy is even more pronounced. Our findings suggest that halo populations observed under the lensing category cannot be fully explained by dark matter alone; they likely involve a substantial contribution from baryons. To better predict these halos, our research suggests incorporating the effects of stochastic fluctuations on a mesoscale level. We also explored modifications to the concentration-halo mass relationship, the halo mass distribution, the impact of mergers, and the consequences for the halo spin distribution and the relationship between halo mass and concentration. Our analysis highlights the limitations of the density-only model and the potential of using halo mesoscale statistics as observational data to support the support the case for stochastic fluctuations influencing the formation of massive halos.

The newly introduced 'analog fluid' approach to studying rotating stars permits researchers to apply complex fluid dynamics theories to investigate rotating stellar objects by assigning properties, such as mass and angular momentum, to individual particles within a fluid, maintaining consistency with conservation laws for mass and angular momentum. This method retains compatibility with established methods for modeling slowly rotating stars. This study develops and tests an analog fluid pseudo-spectral solver in two dimensions, demonstrating that it produces results almost identical to those of a traditional pseudo-spectral solver when stars rotate at low speeds. Furthermore, it accurately reproduces patterns of angular momentum redistribution in rotating stars. This solver is designed to be easily adaptable for three-dimensional simulations of rotating stars with minimal reconfiguration.

Acquiring extensive, high-quality data is a costly and time-consuming process that can be streamlined through active learning techniques, specifically by focusing efforts on labeling data most likely to provide new insights to the model. While various approaches have been proposed, they often depend on efficient pre-training models and are limited in models without such capabilities, or when the available unlabeled data does not fully represent the data distribution we are interested in, but can be tackled effectively by a novel method called Importance-Sampling-Based Active Learning, or ISAL, which, in comparison, tends to outperform conventional algorithms. Furthermore, ISAL is flexible, offering various advantages such as the ability to seamlessly incorporate data pre-training, handling scenarios where only partial and noisy information is available about the available unlabeled data, and when combined with efficient training algorithms like CREST, it delivers notable performance gains by a factor of ten, in our experiments, nearly 50, in comparison to conventional methods.

For the first time, a specific type of neutron star has been identified as capable of producing electromagnetic radiation detectable on Earth during the process of gravitational and electromagnetic co-detection in gravitational wave detectors. This discovery was made based on observations from multiple sources, including NASA's Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer, the European Space Agency's ITO satellite, and ground-based electromagnetic detectors, following the detection of a gravitational wave event by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations. By analyzing these observations, scientists are now able to accurately determine the electromagnetic local horizon radius of these neutron stars and predict the range in which star formation events could give rise to bright supernovae explosions.

The global pandemic highlighted the critical need for clear, effective public communication and the importance of urban diversity in everyday interactions. While initial studies examined various aspects of urban life during lockdowns, the lasting impacts remain poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce a new, adjustable metric called $c$-diversity to quantify the variety of activities, service usages, and demographic mix in urban settings. By analyzing data from over 10 million Google Trends queries in 1,500 major cities worldwide, we track changes in urban diversity from early 2020 through 2021. Our study reveals that despite variations across regions and city sizes, many cities experienced reduced diversity well into 2021. Furthermore, we found that cities in the Global South and smaller cities showed $c$-diversity reductions that were less pronounced than in their larger counterparts. The results also suggest that certain factors, including necessary health measures, contributed to increased monoculture in some cities, but not others. Ultimately, our study provides valuable insights for urban planners and policymakers in promoting diversity, which is key to building resilient communities.

The objects within the inner region of high mass young stellar objects are often surrounded by thin rings and are believed to be responsible for modifying the dynamics of the inner disc. To better understand the interactions between these objects and the inner disc, a novel numerical model has been developed using the 'gh4d' code to simulate the migration of two massive objects within a high mass young stellar object environment - specifically, one object with 1.5 times the mass of the Sun and another with 3 times the mass of the Sun - within a young stellar environment known as L1536. Through numerical modeling, the migration of these objects has been captured, even the less massive object, in a comprehensive multi-object multi-disc simulation. The model demonstrates that the interaction between the objects and the inner disc results in several distinct features that have been observed in spectral lines of atomic hydrogen - including matter being ejected from the accretion disc of the more massive object, material being transferred from the accretion disc to the smaller object, and extensive heating of the inner disc that causes significant emission from atomic hydrogen. Notably, the model also reveals that the objects within the inner disc appear as distinct bright spots that have very different characteristics than what has been previously observed in the spectrum of L1536 - such as one bright spot exhibiting strong water lines in the mid-infrared, while the other exhibits primarily atomic hydrogen and mid-infrared continuum - such as in the system of L1536.

A numerical method based on high-order spectral transformation is developed to calculate horizontal and vertical surface elevations and pressure from a given wave envelope. This approach holds a particular value in turbulent flow simulations, where only the surface elevation and limited interior data may be accessible, enabling the reconstruction of the free surface shape based on pressure information at several interior points. The described method's surface reconstruction data is utilized in a study on irregular wave run-up on an vertical wall, with a high-order spectral algorithm calculating surface elevation and surface pressure from the envelope provided by a specific empirical model. The resulting data allows for the determination of the surface shape, and when paired with unsteady Bernoulli's equation, enables the calculation of pressure at the water surface based on interior pressure data measured by pressure transducers, and this calculation is then compared to direct pressure transducer measurements to validate its accuracy.

A new extension of Morley's surface layer theorem for differentiable differential forms is demonstrated in this work, by first establishing a foundation with Preiss's theorem on the surface measure, then building on this with a theorem about differential forms.

This article presents a method for managing mobile devices with sonar sensors,, equipping each layer with distinct functions, and facilitating the creation and modification of individual layers. The proposed system consists of a modular layered control framework that connects different layers through standardized interfaces. The primary purpose of layer Layer N is to detect new objects and update the information gathered about them. The system also includes sonar data integration, and framework that enables efficient utilization of data by analyzing the reliability of individual sensors and combining them accordingly. The paper presents experimental findings related to the frame and sonar data integration, demonstrating their effectiveness through practical applications.

A surge in dissemination of deceptive and misleading information through
social media platforms poses significant challenges and poses threats to
democratic processes worldwide. This investigation into the effectiveness of
machine learning techniques for identifying fake news focuses on the impact
of training models without incorporating contextual elements. Beginning with
the state-of-the-art neural baseline, our analysis investigates the performance
degradation when key information types are excluded. Our research reveals
that current models are skewed toward certain indicators and lacks diversity,
and is particularly over-reliant on textual content. Furthermore, we propose
a fake news detection model utilizing auxiliary information from browser plugins
to gather URL domain information, and evaluates its utility in comparison to
other available indicators. Our comparative analysis of bibliography tools
and their impact on user perceptions of news credibility forms the foundation
for this approach. Our model incorporates readily accessible page metadata
into its analysis. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating
 contextual information in detecting false information and provide valuable
insights into the mechanisms underlying current deep learning methods used
for this purpose.

We investigated the impact of curvature on the mean-field Ising model,
incorporating a mechanism where the number of a spin's neighbors with the same
orientation determines its likelihood of flipping, in addition to the typical
magnetic ordering forces. This design allows us to incorporate the effects of
curvature in two dimensions. The model exhibits features reminiscent of causal
dynamics and general relativity. As the temperature rises, the effect of
curvature results in the back-reaction that generates the Bardeyn-Λ phase
transition. As the temperature drops, the effect of curvature leads to the
emergence of an ordered state that opposes the magnetic ordering, resulting
in the hysteresis. These results indicate that the mean-field Ising model with
two-dimensional interaction can effectively incorporate the effects of
diffuse matter-gravity coupling.

This paper addresses the $l_1$-PCA optimization problem with two variable blocks following a rotationally invariant transformation. We present an algorithm based on coordinate blocks refinement that alternates between two variable blocks using alternating minimization. By analyzing the problem as a non-convex optimization task, we establish convergence to a stationary point. Numerical results demonstrate convergence to a high precision solution and showcase application to actual data. An efficient implementation is also demonstrated.

This paper introduces a novel approach to semantic labeling annotation, focusing on ensuring the consistency of annotated labels through a new class of consistent sentences. We establish a theoretical framework for this approach by dividing the consistency task into two distinct problems: label permutation and fact checking. Our proposed method leverages deep neural networks to address these problems, and extensive experiments on large datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in validating the accuracy of semantic labeling annotations.

Our hi-resolution map system, known as HiTMap, presents a novel approach that integrates both place-based and global metric navigation within the same framework.  This system utilizes a hierarchical representation consisting of a wide-area framework and multiple independent metric maps, developed and maintained by independent agents without exchanging information.  These independent agents are capable of seamlessly transferring high-resolution maps between one another to facilitate efficient goal-directed navigation.  To validate our concept, an agent-based platform called HiTAgent was created, featuring independent modules that build and navigate using hiTMap representations, effortlessly transferring between one another.  This module's capability to locate new goals beyond the range of its individual map was demonstrated, showcasing the system's effectiveness.  All findings were published with corresponding code available for review.

A recent experiment used atomic interferometry to detect a small magnetic field in the laboratory. This field, which was unknown and not shielded from the experiment's setup, was detected with such precision that it could measure values as low as $0.4$ nT over a wide frequency range. The measurement also revealed how this field varied over time and space, providing valuable information for designing better atomic clocks and for detecting gravitational waves.

This study develops an alternative statistical modeling approach to admixture analysis, focusing on alternatives to traditional methods. A new model is introduced, replacing component identification with density estimation, and employs a Dirichlet process prior. The model is suitable for scenarios with many possible admixture compositions, and does not require components to match those of the source populations. Simulation studies compare the new model to existing methods, and findings are applied to a genetics case study involving Neanderthal admixture analysis. Using high-quality simulant data, the new model accurately retrieves the Neanderthal component, and when applied to older data with a single-point mutation type, the Neanderthal component is successfully identified.

GPU programming sees significant advancements, particularly in solving time complexity issues, but current GPU memory allocation methods suffer from inefficiencies due to frequent memory reallocations and fragmentation. These issues are especially pronounced when developing iterative solutions with allocation-based time complexity. We present DynaSOAr, an innovative GPU memory allocator designed to minimize memory fragmentation and enhance allocation speed, specifically for iterations with allocation-based time complexity. Unlike conventional methods, DynaSOAr leverages GPU memory pre-reservation, enabling thread-safe memory allocation and reuse, which prevents fragmentation and enables time complexity forecasting. Evaluated across diverse applications, including graph algorithms and machine learning, our research shows that DynaSOAr maintains efficiency and accuracy while outperforming state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators (mimalloc-gpu and cudaMallocAsync) by 1.37 to 20 times in speed, and offering an 11 to $O(n)$ fold improvement for problems with allocation-based time complexity. Moreover, DynaSOAr avoids memory fragmentation, allowing the same GPU memory to be released and reused without performance degradation or memory leakage. All code for our tests and the DynaSOAr allocator is available on GitHub.

The influence of magnetic adatoms and dimer in a lead monolayer on the behavior of a spin singlet state in an Al-Sc trimer has been analyzed theoretically. The magnetic adatoms and dimer were found to significantly impact the location of the YSR state peaks in the local density of spin. Notably, the exchange interaction between the Ysr state peaks in a magnetic dimer or adatoms can occur, although this effect is relatively small. The study also explored the magnetic adatom/dimer placement at different lattice sites and how the proximity to the Al-Sc dimer influenced the number of adatoms required to move a peak in the local density of states (LDOS). Furthermore, the research identified the presence of magnetic moments and their behavior with respect to the local magnetic field in their vicinity and away from it, as well as the necessary adatom/dimer configuration to generate a magnetic moment and the exchange interaction within a ring current.

A comprehensive analysis of a 9-year light curve from the TRAPPIST star system has revealed subtle periodic changes in the brightness of stars, potentially caused by long-period planets or distant companions. A blend of orbital models and spectral analysis has helped scientists differentiate between subtle endogenous effects and an interaction between TRAPPIST-1 and the planet TRAPPIST-1b that results in tidal heating. This interaction may have led to a significant increase in the planet's rotational speed and could potentially explain the planet's atmospheric properties. Furthermore, researchers have also discovered evidence of possible low-altitude cloud cover on three of the planets, as well as an explanation for the anomalous rotation of TRAPPIST-1b based on an interaction with a massive asteroid or comet. If confirmed, these findings would provide valuable insights into the behavior of transiting mini-Neptunes located within the "habitable zone".

The substitution of Ti with C and N in rutile TiO2 and the corresponding configurations have been analyzed. Substituting Ti with either C or N results in a net gain of electrons, with this effect being more pronounced in the case of N-doping. N-deficient TiO2 exhibits a semiconducting characteristic with a low defect state localization. Conversely, Ti-doped TiO2 exhibits states within the band gap, where these states become occupied under low defect conditions, leading to metallic behavior. It is found that carbon and nitrogen atoms in interstitial positions tend to acquire electrons from surrounding Ti atoms, with this effect being more pronounced in the case of interstitial N. The vibrational frequencies of C and N defects are more noticeable in substitutional configurations than in interstitial ones. Notably, N-deficient TiO2 exhibits a position in the Ti-doped band gap when situated near a Ti atom in an octahedral arrangement.

Top quark decays into other types of quarks through a process known as flavor changing neutral current are strictly prohibited by the Standard Model, making them highly sensitive to potential new physics. In order to identify possible sources of unexpected physics within the reach of the Large Hadron Collider, in searches for FNC decays, theoretical predictions for top quark decay into bottom and strange quarks suggest that for certain channels, the branching ratios may exceed the expected limits at 95% confidence level. In contrast, for charged quarks, the branching ratios are anticipated to be higher and more accessible. In this study, in the search for the process $t \rightarrow q + W^{-}$, with $q = (d, s, b)$, the maximum allowable branching ratios for the Large Hadron Hadron Collider are found to be significantly lower than those for the upcoming Large Hadron Hadron Collider, which could disapprove of certain types of new physics within a specific mass range. In this analysis, in the associated production of a top quark with a Higgs boson or two Higgs bosons, the branching ratios for the following processes are investigated, which include $t \rightarrow b + W^-$, $t \rightarrow s + W^-$, $t \rightarrow s + \gamma$, $t \rightarrow b + \gamma$, $t \rightarrow b + b \bar{b}$, $t \rightarrow s + s \bar{s}$, and

This research tackles a significant challenge in combinatorial edge-coloring problems. For a graph with edge-colored boundaries, δ-r colored edges are assigned a specific color from a range of 1 to δ, finding lower bounds for this range based on the graph's structure. Initially, Guo and Huang established a (n-2)r lower bound for an n vertex directed graph. Subsequently, several researchers built upon this work. Our contribution builds upon their findings by proving a more rigorous lower bound, r≥n over a more comprehensive class of graphs. Specifically, our proof utilizes the Jordan curve lemma to analyze a triangle, establishing a lower bound of r≥3 over a triangle's graph class. Our findings also hold for more complex graph structures derived from a triangle through operations like edge rotation and vertex merging. Our breakthrough is also applicable to directed graphs and resolves an earlier conjecture by combinatorial researchers.

We investigate mass determination for a free scalar field in a circular cavity with an irregular cavity shape, using nohson-perthurbative methods to second order. Analyzing the nohson spectral density in the irregular cavity, we both graphically and analytically characterize its properties, focusing on the main channel and three subchannels, each tailored to specific noise types - phase damping, amplitude damping, amplitude and phase damping, and decoherence. Our nohson spectral density findings lead to mass shift determinations for the free scalar field under these irregular cavity conditions. Notably, our mass shift determinations show that qubits with nohson and amplitude and phase damping nohse tolerate higher mass thresholds than qutrits, whereas qutrits outperform in phase damping and amplitude damping scenarios, with tolerance decreasing as nohson frequency increases in all cases.

Recent measurements indicate that the polarization of positrons collected from a 7 GeV photon beam, interacting with linearly polarized electrons at the HEPL facility, is around 10%. In comparison, the degree of polarization can exceed 30% in positrons produced from $e^+e^-$ colliders and has reached levels greater than 80% in certain $p$-$\bar{p}$ collisions. For certain applications, a high level of polarization in these particles is necessary. For potential application in a linear $p$-$\bar{p}$ polarized collider, there's a requirement for the polarization of 80% in 7 GeV in the transverse plane. A novel method is proposed to achieve more than 30% polarization in these positrons using a Red-Shifted Plasma Undulator (RPU). The primary concept of RPU involves injecting a positron bunch into a plasma undulator with a reduced photon frequency, moving in the opposite direction to the motion of the positrons.

We demonstrate that all groups with polynomial diameter properties have an infinite number of non-trivial conjugacy classes, contain no infinite nilpotent subprojects, and specifically cannot from a finite quotient. In contrast, the free group in two generators has no such property from its polynomial diameter.

This paper describes the creation of a digital temperature sensor with a proposed
resolution of 0.01 degrees Celsius and inaccuracies less than 1 degree Celsius,
utilizing an inexpensive temperature-to-digital conversion IC and a high-precision
reference voltage generator. The design, mainly concentrated on software, employs
an iterative algorithm in its second step to compensate for non-linear temperature
behavior and achieve linear temperature sensing. The sensor's architecture is
simple and requires a minimal number of external components, making it suitable
for a wide range of temperatures and inaccuracies, which are demonstrated to be
effective across different temperatures.

Topological groupoid expansions form a topological equivalent to the concept of expansions in topological stacks. Building on this, we introduce the correspondences between gerbes over a topological stack and certain actions within that stack, also in a topological setting. These relationships then allow us to characterize the fundamental properties of the functor establishing the connection between the categories of topological groupoids and topological stacks, as well as the exact sequence definitions within the broader framework.

zonal function $Z_\sigma^{(\alpha)}(t)$ in the variable t results in expressing 
another zonal function $Z_\tau^{(\alpha)}(\tau)$ in the same variable t for 
given parameters $\sigma$, $\alpha$ and t. It is found that conventional 
differentiation and integration integration disrupt the positive definiteness 
property of the function class, thereby complicating these operations. Nevertheless, 
specific formulas are derived for the integrated and integrated by parts cases 
that maintain the property of being a zonal function, and under certain

A key parameter that is used to characterize the Moult effect in liquid foams is the roughness factor, which is made up of two components that represent the first and second moments of the angle distribution of the foam's interface.  This paper employs theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to determine the range in which the roughness factor can be found in foams that have been given an initial horizontal orientation and then oriented vertically.  It is found that a single component of the roughness factor is uniform throughout the foam when it is horizontal, but when the foam is oriented vertically this component varies with position.  This paper also demonstrates that there are two distinct behaviors that the roughness factor can exhibit in the vertical orientation depending on the relationship between the gravity number and the dimensionless flow rate.  It is found that for low values of these parameters, the roughness factor is uniform with position, but for higher values of these parameters, the roughness factor is composed of two parts that are separated by a breakpoint that is determined by the relationship between these parameters.  This paper has significant implications for understanding the behaviour of foams in real-world applications such as food processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Recently, deep neural network ensembles have shown a significant performance increase, particularly when applied to individual network improvements. While the concept of ensembles isn't new, applying them to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has faced challenges due to size and speed constraints. Despite this, the application of ensembles in CNNs continues to yield superior results. In our study, we explore a novel approach to creating CNN ensembles that leverages small, lightweight networks with varying compression and pruning levels, resulting in a network ensemble that offers enhanced accuracy compared to larger networks, and can be trained efficiently on a single GPU. Specifically, our method comprises four distinct approaches that utilize networks with different characteristics, and when combined, produce superior accuracy similar to that of significantly bigger networks, and with the added benefit of training efficiency on hardware with limited resources.

We employ a computationally intensive method to simulate the various behaviors exhibited by a rotating milk-like fluid in a thin chamber, specifically focusing on the Taylor-Helical experiments. By both theoretically and numerically scrutinizing the interactions between surface tension and membrane tension, we reveal how these forces compete with each other. Notably, even at very small radii where analytical methods fall short, we discover that surface tension promotes rotational stability while membrane tension drives rotational instability. Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights for applications ranging from microfluidics to the study of biological cells.

A detailed investigation of cyclopentadiene (C5H6) abundance and its connection to stable isomers like benzyne has been undertaken. A new rotational spectrum in the 40-60 GHz range has been discovered and assigned to the zero vibrational state of its ground electronic state. Abundance estimates for cyclopentadiene and its ion, in comparison to the ionized forms of CN derivatives, have been made and indicate a higher cyclopentadiene abundance relative to benzyne, in contrast to the comparison between cyclobutadiene and cyclopropenyl ions. The reasons behind this cyclobutadiene to benzyne abundance ratio have been explored. Furthermore, theoretical calculations of dipole moments for cyclopentadiene isomers have been carried out and compared with experimental data and other theoretical predictions.

Our paper proposes a novel look-ahead attention mechanism for neural machine translation, an innovation that builds upon the conventional look-ahead attention by incorporating a forward prediction of the source sentence's remaining parts. This is done to rapidly predict the next target sentence character during decoding. We believe that predicting the next source sentence part, rather than just a position, more accurately reflects the nature of attention in NMT. Our approach requires no training changes and shows significant improvements over the baseline and the existing look-ahead attention model on three language pairs, with the benefit of extending the speed of NMT character generation by up to 2.5 times. Our achievement has been recognized at the Findings of EMNLP 2020 conference.

A lambda-scalar field model is proposed for an open universe, utilizing a polynomial inflationary potential and expressed within a fractional calculus framework to analyze its behavior. The model's parameters are determined by solving the Fokker-Planck equation, with results showing that the model's viscosity coefficient is directly correlated with the scalar field's average value. Compared to other models with similar potential functions, this model evolves with a higher viscosity coefficient, while it is shrank in terms of its inflaton field. The model's dynamics are further illustrated through the use of phase portraits and correlation functions, with additional insights gained from analyzing the lambda-scalar field model's likelihood and information entropy.

Researchers have constrained the interaction between dark matter and nucleons through atomic recoil experiments, and possibly through the decay of the $J/$$\psi$ particle into invisible particles, but the latter method may be less effective due to the small size of its cross-section. To address this issue, we focus on increasing the impact of the invisible J/$$\psi$$ decay channel by utilizing hadron initiators in a next-generation electron-positron collider like the Linear Collider. By employing initial state radiation with a high-energy beam of 500 GeV, we can achieve limits on dark matter scattering that are comparable to, or even surpass, the current records set by atomic recoil experiments for certain mass ranges. We discover that we can constrain the scattering cross-section for a dark matter particle of 5 GeV with a tens of picobarn limit, and for a 100 GeV particle, we can reach limits of a few femtobarns. These results are highly dependent on production cross-section calculations, hadron decay simulations, and the detection of neutral hadrons within the final state. We also analyze the influence of the hadron physics and experimental conditions on our results.

MFSSA is an advanced version of SSA that uses factor analysis to its core steps, allowing for 3D representation of time series data and its applications in various fields, including remote sensing and financial analysis. In this study, we explore the use of MFSSA for analyzing temperature curves and remote sensing images. For these applications, we modify the MF algorithm to its iterative version, utilizing its 3D time series representation to develop efficient reassignment rules that leverage data information. Numerical results demonstrate that MFSSA effectively separates temperature curves and separates images with and without the cloud cover.

Let I be a measure that represents the distribution of random walk steps. For b greater than zero, let I_b denote the measure derived from I, weighted according to its tail to the b power. This work establishes that as n approaches infinity, the sum of the random walk steps scaled by a factor of n to the power of 1 plus b over 2 will distribute in a manner that matches a standard normal distribution. The validity of this asymptotic result relies on the value of b falling within the range (0, 2). The proof strategy involves constructing the random walk with i.i.d. steps conditioned by tail weights b and utilizing compactness properties of probability measures in the work undertaken by Chatterjee and Ghosal. The establishment of this asymptotic behavior is shown to hold true when considering the range (0, 2) for b, and it is worth noting that for b values greater than two, the asymptotic distribution is influenced by the characteristic function of the steps' distribution.

The efficiency of plasma sources is closely tied to key factors, including the plasma temperature and density, which vary across different locations. This is crucial for developing sources that are precise and reliable for multiple applications simultaneously. In order to reduce complex plasma systems for specific uses, it's vital to understand how key parameters, including the density, are related. This study presents an investigation into a radio frequency plasma source with a 100 mm chamber, where samples were collected from different areas, and a ratio of the rate of sample collection to the rate of plasma gas intake of 150 was maintained. By comparing plasma characteristics obtained from different locations with each other and over time, researchers found that comparing plasma features by looking at their spectral signatures is more effective than traditional methods for identifying the relationship between features and parameters. This study reveals that the ratio of two signature features can accurately predict the density in different areas of the chamber, offering a simplified way to model the density distribution and develop sources that are accurate in multiple areas at the same time.

The proposed W-shaped network (WSNet) is a novel deep learning framework that
is especially effective for automatic nucleus detection in images with high levels
of noise and low contrast.  To start, we use a compact U-Net to detect the
nuclei in a given image.  The results then feed into two stages of refinement:
mask refinement using a Generative Adversarial Network and post-processing with
a Regression Adversarial Network.  What makes WSNet so efficient is that it can
accurately identify nuclei in images that are difficult to process, without the
need for time-consuming image segmentation pretraining.  What's more, WSNet's
innovative design leverages the power of attention mechanisms, residual learning,
generative adversarial networks, and post-processing to deliver superior results.

This survey article provides an in-depth examination of the local gamma factors associated with representations of a non-Archimedean field by an element of the family of orthogonal or symplectic groups. It summarizes the rank of these gamma factors, which is shown to be Isom, reflecting the isomorphism of such representations. These results are critical for proving the Gross Primitives Conjecture and the Base Change Theorem for automorphic representations within the specified categories.

With recent breakthroughs in deep graph neural networks, the community has made significant progress, yet traditional CNN and fully connected Neural Networks (NNs) can be seen as special cases on highly structured graphs, as demonstrated by our work. We provide a unified mathematical framework for these networks, detailing how they all rely on graph convolutions based on neural adjacency matrices and degree normalization matrices, as well as volume preservation through gradient backpropagation analysis. Our approach also reveals that both CNN and fully connected NN operations are essentially composed of multiple convolutional and activation layers, along with implicit bias terms present in every layer. This explanation offers a new perspective that may inspire novel CNN architecture designs and help clarify the underlying mechanisms of their effectiveness in training, as demonstrated by successfully rederiving standard CNN and fully connected NN training procedures based solely on graph convolution and layer training cycles.

A new theory known as "hairy" gravity has emerged, which includes general relativity as a special case and is characterized by adding a finite number of terms to the Einstein-Hilbert action. Researchers have recently studied the thermodynamic properties of hairy black holes within this theory, specifically analyzing their entropy, specific heat, and phase transitions, which can become even more complex when the black holes possess multiple hair parameters. Furthermore, the authors have investigated the relationship between the thermodynamic behavior of rotating hairy black holes and the theory in pure gravity. Notably, they found that by redefining the hairy parameters, the thermodynamic behavior of these black holes mirror that of pure gravity, which implies that the entropy of a rotating hairy black hole has a direct correlation with the area of its event horizon, thus supporting the Bekenstein-Hawking conjecture. However, this relationship does not hold for non-rotating hairy black holes, which exhibit entropies that depend on the horizon area to the power of two.

Research into elastography has primarily focused on reducing lateral estimation errors, largely neglecting axial displacement errors. Yet, given that ultrasound imaging provides higher resolution axially compared to laterally, accurate elastography would necessely place greater emphasis on axial accuracy. This paper thus aims to improve axial elastography methods by addressing the significant challenge of speckle noise, particularly in cases with high displacement estimates. To tackle this, a novel two-stage approach is introduced. The initial phase employs a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) to clean interpolated frames, building on an elastic registration to align target and source frames. In the second phase, refined flow fields are obtained through a semi-supervised learning model utilizing spatially varying confidence maps to handle large flow fields. Evaluations using highly elastic phantoms with high-resolution shear waves show significantly improved axial displacement errors when utilizing 20% elastic samples and 800 frame cleanings, particularly in highly noisy conditions with high frame rates, as well as substantial reductions in lateral displacement errors.

Logical pseudocodes, a novel approach to correctly and safely specifying
behaviors for algorithms, are presented as a means to correctly algorithms'
correctness and safety without correctly or safely indicating how to
achieve their desired outcomes. From the perspectives of correctness and safety,
logical pseudocodes can be viewed as a bridge between abstract specifications
and formal correctness/safety proofs. A set of guidelines is provided to produce
logical pseudocdes that correctly and safely specify the behaviors for alternative
data structures, program commands, and programs themselves. This approach is
particularly useful in validating programs written in correctly and safely
verification tools like CVC4, ALPINE, and VeriFi. By utilizing this method,
key elements such as memory management in pointers, pointer manipulation in
dynamically managed data structures, complex program programs, and a set of programs
involving multiple cases of programs alternative data structures can be easily
specified and verified, as shown by examples in different verification tools.

This paper presents a one-pass algorithm for approximating $k$-means clustering in high-dimensional space, utilizing a coreset construction method. The algorithm, which maintains a set of data points, achieves an approximation ratio of $(1\+\Omega(1))k$-means with dimension reduction, and does so while managing memory efficiently. The performance of the algorithm is assessed as it depends on the number of data points processed, the desired accuracy, and the dimension of the space, but not significantly on $k$. Compared to existing methods, this algorithm offers an improved dependency on $k$ and allows for the use of state-of-the-art coreset algorithms after the initial step.

We propose a method that breaks down the N x M grid into larger states and assigns a distinct Markov Decision Process to each state, reducing the complexity of a finite-state model by replacing $NM2^{KM}$ states with $NM + K$ states and reducing transitions from $NM(KM)$ to $NM + K(KM)$ when $K > M$. We apply this concept to a pursuit-evasion scenario with $N$ chasers and $K$ runners on an $N \times M$ grid, and demonstrate that dividing the environment into superstates significantly reduces the entropy of states, particularly in large-scale instances where precise estimation of state entropy becomes challenging. Furthermore, utilizing these reductions, we successfully solve and visualize strategically valuable instances that were previously beyond computational reach.

At the $\mathcal{N}$-th loop level, the Z-boson and W-boson distribution patterns are anticipated to contain an inherent component, which is unaffected by polarization effects, particularly for the $\mathcal{Q}^2$ values beyond their mass squared ($\mathcal{Q}^2 \gg M^2_{Z/W}$). To the $\mathcal{N}$th loop level, the universal component is found to be nearly the same as the massless limit of the Z-boson and W-boson distributions. Nevertheless, the $\mathcal{Q}^2$ values below the Z/W-mass squared values ($\mathcal{Q}^2 \ll M^2_{Z/W}$) exhibit distinct features due to polarization effects, which become negligible in the $\textrm{BSM}$ scenario with massless Z/W-bosons. These differences, which are represented by the differences between the Z/W-boson distributions and the massless limit, are shown in the presented results for the Z-boson and W-boson distributions at the $\mathcal{N}$-LL level, derived from the $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^2)$ corrections. The Z-boson distribution displays a negligible difference between polarized and non-polarized distributions, whereas the Z-boson distribution shows a more pronounced difference, which the Z/W-boson distribution partially matches

In this study, we focus on a key challenge in the real world: teaching an agent to navigate complex, changing environments by allowing it to compare multiple model representations during a multi-task reinforcement learning process. To achieve this, we develop a novel algorithm called HATD (Hybrid Attention Dynamics Model) that utilizes a mechanism to dynamically select the most relevant parts of several learned models when making value predictions. However, due to the potential risk that the agent might develop a preference for a specific dynamics model during the training phase, we also create an external comparison system using multiple dynamics models to prevent such behavior. Training HATD involves integrating this comparison system, the set of learned dynamics models, and a diverse collection of reward signals during the training process. As a byproduct, this method also serves as an effective solution for single-task reinforcement learning problems. We demonstrate the advantages of HATD by applying it across various multi-task learning scenarios and showing that it outperforms both traditional and contemporary learning algorithms.

In 1932, Joseph Rosser enhanced Godel's first incompleteness theorem by proving that within any formal system capable of expressing basic arithmetic, there is either an affirmative or negative statement that cannot be shown to be true or false based on the system's axioms alone. This argument holds for cases where it is difficult or impossible to determine the truth of statements from a logical system based on external information. We will explore the concepts underlying the Godel sentence, the assumptions required for the application of the first incompleteness theorem, and the implications if formal systems have the capacity to represent themselves.

A generalized version of Hadamard's three circles theorem is proven for monogenic functions in spaces with more than one dimension. The proof leverages the connection between the circular mean of monogenic functions and their value at the center, which is also used to establish the reverse inequality in the theorem.

Imaging applications often require generating samples that account for some additional information based on an initial prior model. Traditional methods achieve this by estimating a reweighting function, which can be computationally intensive due to the large size of image volumes. In this paper, we introduce a novel and efficient way to generate image volumes using a conditional Wasserstein GAN that is enhanced with a gradient normalization component. This method allows us to bypass the need for handling input information as grayscale maps by simply feeding it in a binary format, indicating areas that should be affected. We test this technique by applying it to fill in missing parts of MRI images using ultrasound data, and also explore its potential in other scenarios requiring precise local control. Additionally, we are able to generate varying levels of information influence through a simple and easy to implement weighting scheme.

This research examines the criteria required for linear subspaces within complex fractional order systems to maintain invariance. It derives essential conditions for a system to possess certain linear invariant subspaces and introduces the concept of a fractional order core for reachability spaces. The relationship between reachable spaces of adjoint systems is also investigated. The theoretical findings are demonstrated through the analysis of a bioreactor model under fractional order dynamics.

Recent observations of the radio pulsar PSR B1133+16, conducted with the Very Large Array, reveal that the planet-like effects are caused by several distinct, individual scattering screens rather than just one. A total of 10 such screens, located at various distances, were pinpointed, with their own unique characteristics of their own. Most of these screens are situated between 1.0 and 5.0 parsecs from our location, with their own unique distances, locations, and associated parameters. The results of these observations uncover that even short-term variations in the radio frequency range can provide valuable information about the distribution of electrons in space and can also disclose details about the movements of the radio pulsar itself. Comparing these observations with previous observations conducted with the Arecibo Observatory in 1993, reveals that the overall nature of scattering has remained largely unaltered over the past 30 years, with only the most closely located screen potentially providing a different outcome.

This paper proposes a innovative method for signal analysis by combining two convolutional layers in a cascaded configuration. In the first stage, dilated convolutional layers extract the periodic component of a signal, and then the second stage captures the quasi-periodic variations through convolution. To test our hypothesis, we focus on modeling speech as a primary example. Experimental results show that our proposed architecture significantly outperforms the original Conv-Pyramid in modeling speech signals and achieves nearly the same performance as the state-of-the-art Net-Joint model.

This paper presents original computations of topological Hochschild homology for a specific algebraic structure known as the Berman-Morel basic class, which can be toped using a bi-categorical structure. Initially shown by Berman and Morel to have a simple topological homology in its first few dimensions, this structure's topological homology is precisely described here as having a specific algebraic property. To achieve this result, we extend the bi-categorical structure to a higher level, which then allows us to use a related functor to compute its bi-categorical shadow, effectively mirroring the bi-categorical structure in a simplified form.

The visual world can be navigated with the help of source localization, where the source of a sound is identified visually. VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) is a new sound source localization benchmark based on the ImageNet dataset, where images are classified according to whether they contain certain sounds. This benchmark was proposed to replace the current data-sparse and modality-sparse datasets used in cross-modal source localization research. The VGG-SS benchmark consists of 10,000 labeled images associated with 500 sound classes from the VGGSound dataset, covering diverse objects across 211 object categories. We collected and annotated the VGG-SS data using the VGGSound app, which facilitates the collection of data and allows users to rate the salience of sound-object associations. We evaluated several cross-modal source localization models using the VGG-SS benchmark, including models trained on highly related and dissimilar modalities, and found that the most effective approach is one that leverages training on both modalities, and that the VGG-SS benchmark is more challenging than the current state-of-the-art datasets due to its diverse range of objects and the presence of sound objects that are not associated with any particular source.

Current hyperbolic graph convolutional network (GCN) variants primarily exploit the property of Hirschberger space to leverage the non-Euclidean layout of data within graph structures.  However, these methods fail to fully utilize the advantageous features of Hirschberger space for graph node feature representation.  We introduce a novel hyperbolic GCN model called LGCN that effectively harnesses these features by incorporating the two distinct components of the Hirschberger space: the lens-shaped component of Lorentzian space enables the preservation of graph transitivity through Lorentzian metric operations, while the hyperbolic component allows for efficient representation of power-law distributions found in real-world graphs.  We further refine the network by integrating a novel convolutional layer that takes advantage of the hyperbolic component's efficiency. Experimental evaluations on graph classification and link prediction tasks using real-world graphs demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing hyperbolic GCN methods, as well as in the Euclidean and general GCN frameworks.

This research focuses on the inverse problem associated with a certain class of PDEs featuring a nonlocal operator called the Ifrim-Shouta derivative. We first establish the uniqueness of solutions to the inverse problem, under specific boundary and source term conditions. To achieve this, we derive an observability inequality from the solution. Furthermore, under the same conditions, the solution is shown to possess a specific regularity property. As a result, the inverse problem is well-posed.

The concept of equilibrium in social systems is discussed with reference to the principles of nonextensive statistical mechanics. Based on the formalism of nonextensive statistical mechanics, we introduce the idea of a "quasiequilibrium" state in society. Furthermore, we employ the maximum Tsallis entropy method to derive the full set of nonextensive hydrodynamic equations governing the time-dependent behavior of a society. These equations comprise the Tsallis distribution, an exponential decay law for the nonextensive parameter, and nonextensive hydrodynamic pressures and viscosities. The significance of our approach lies in its use of nonextensive statistical mechanics to enable a hydrodynamic description of societal evolution, thus connecting the principles of nonextensive statistical mechanics with those of nonextensive hydrodynamics in a real-world context.

This study examines the linearized gravitational perturbations resulting from a massive source in de Sitter spacetime, focusing on the case where the perturbation equation includes a mass term. By deriving solutions through a linear combination of de Sitter harmonics in a general coordinate system, we obtain explicit mass-term solutions that align with previously established results from alternative methodologies. Additionally, we establish the equivalence between the gauge-invariant formalism and the Regge-Teuerita approach for perturbations in the traceless-transverse gauge. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adding a mass term reduces gravity's linearized degrees of freedom from two to one. Furthermore, we establish the existence of massive de Sitter harmonics with discrete masses and angular numbers, which are crucial in forming a complete, complete, and bi-orthogonal set of harmonic functions.

We perform a classification of Hamiltonian dynamics in four categories based on their behavior in the long run, for Hamiltonians with absolutely continuous spectral measure, within the context of quantum equilibrium states. Each category corresponds to a reversible or irreversible process, with further subdivision based on whether entropy changes over time. We demonstrate that the classification is equivalent to another criterion involving the relationship between the density of a state with respect to its squared form and the spectral measure of the observable defining the state. Additionally, we provide explicit examples of equilibrium states and Hamiltonians that fall into each category, including those modeling radiation, friction, and ballistc or diffusive transport.

Two-level system ensemble members evolve dynamically when influenced by mutual interactions and an external environment, resulting in a possible negative temperature state, identifiable through their population distribution between energy levels. We demonstrate that this system can exhibit negative temperature behavior on a 2x2 lattice with pairwise interactions and/or an influence from an outside field. The condition for the emergence of negative temperature is analytically derived for this system, and its evolution over time is numerically investigated, showing a transition from negative to positive temperature is inevitable as the system interacts with its environment, even if started in a negative temperature state. The relationship between the system's parameters and the positive and negative temperature regions is illustrated through phase diagrams, and the system's temperature evolution is plotted against various interaction and field strength combinations.

This paper investigates theoretical concepts linked to the stability of the vacuum, dark parity symmetry, and the type II seesaw mechanism. We interpret the massive stable particle predicted by the model as a dark matter candidate. To enhance reliability, we integrate a minimal dark sector that interacts with the massive particle but not with ordinary matter. We establish conditions under which the vacuum remains stable and dark parity symmetry disappears. Furthermore, we determine parameters for the new fields that ensure the vacuum is globally stable. The new fields are shown to affect the mass of neutrinos, and we identify parameters where neutrino masses are produced while remaining consistent with experimental data.

We employ a method based on Neumann-Schroder effective Hamiltonians to analyze 
complex crystal field and interaction patterns in transition metal oxides through 
a study of their space-group symmetry. By examining the d-band structure close to 
the Fermi level, we find that the effective spin-orbit coupling strength varies 
considerably across different compounds and can exceed its intrinsic value due to 
combined influences of crystal field effects, charge transfer energy, and 
Sommerfeld expansion terms. For specific cases such as HfO2 and RuSb, we demonstrate that their 
quasi-one-dimensional structures enable the separation of subspaces with distinct 
point-group symmetries. Furthermore, we investigate two independent four-level 
subspaces and show that when interaction terms are neglected and d-electron filling 
is intermediate, large effective spin-orbit coupling values arise, leading to 
point-group dependent effective spin-orbit coupling constants and angular 
momentum operators. We also uncover that some crystal field and angular momentum 
operators effectively commute with the effective Hamiltonian in these subspaces, 
and we derive multiple relationships between effective and intrinsic spin-orbit 
coupling constants. Ultimately, these findings provide detailed insights into how 
specific properties of intermediate valence compounds can be predicted based on 
their structural characteristics.

This research focuses on certain complex geometric shapes known as toric complete intersections, specifically those containing smooth, deeply connected divisor structures. We investigate a specific property called monodromy-invariant relative I-functions for these forms. Our main discovery is that the relative I-functions associated with these forms can be related to one another through a specific type of transformation, similar to how the relative J-functions of such forms have been previously understood. Our proofs use techniques involving the compactification of algebraic varieties defined by equations, local intersection geometry, and quantum torus identities. Our results have practical applications in solving specific algebraic equations and understanding the monodromy of related geometric structures.

A growing number of medical image analysis tasks rely on image manipulation techniques in the training data, but such methods often fail to directly reflect how individual interventions affect a patient's disease state. In this paper, we investigate the impact of latent code adjustments made through generative models on the medical data representation, both locally and globally. Furthermore, we develop a novel approach to refine these latent code changes by utilizing attention maps, which are designed to identify and exclude areas of healthy tissue that are incorrectly classified as affected by a disease. This method, known as Attention-based Latent Code Adjustment (A-LACA), is specifically aimed to produce more accurate predictions when adjusting images of patients with only one side of the body affected by a condition. The effectiveness of A-LACA is demonstrated through simulations on two segmentation tasks using the MRI dataset from the 2021 Privacy Preserving and Enhancing Wavelet Transform (PWET) competition. The results show that A-LACA can yield up to 5.25% better performance than basic latent code adjustment and also have a broader impact on the encoded disease prior when analyzed using Self-supervised Learned Invariant Features (S-LLIF).

Our new platform ViDaExpert is designed to enable users without programming knowledge to work with complex, multidimensional data sets. ViDaExpert achieves this by processing a wide variety of data formats and providing an intuitive 3D data visualization platform. ViDaExpert leverages a pretrained large language model to interpret user requests and seamlessly integrates with external knowledge bases to enhance the accuracy of data visualization. ViDaExpert combines multimodal capabilities to seamlessly work with text, speech, and graphical input methods. Furthermore, ViDaExpert is designed with a modular architecture that allows for easy customization and extension of its functionality to meet the diverse requirements of users working with different types of data sets.
